frameworks.name: Middleware Trap Diagnostic
frameworks.description: A five-step diagnostic test to determine whether a company has a structurally durable AI position or is dangerously dependent on (and thus exposed to absorption by) hyperscaler platforms.
when_to_apply: My AI product depends on OpenAI's API and I'm worried they'll build what we do
We're evaluating an AI startup for investment and need to understand if their moat is real or just execution speed on a borrowed stack
Our board is asking whether AWS or Google could just ship our product as a feature — how do I answer that?
We built a wrapper on top of Claude/GPT and competitors keep launching similar products — should we pivot or double down?
A portfolio company's entire value proposition sits between the foundation model and the end user, and I need to assess how exposed they are
principles: Good execution on the wrong layer of the stack does not create durable competitive advantage
Dependency on a direct competitor's model is a structural fragility, not just a vendor risk
Hyperscaler infrastructure investment creates increasing pressure to absorb middleware value over time
Trust and proprietary domain context can create defensibility that pure orchestration cannot
Absorption risk must be rated at the dependency level, not just assessed holistically
steps: Map every dependency in your product stack (models, APIs, infrastructure providers)
Rate the absorption risk for each dependency — likelihood that the provider builds your functionality natively
Triage your domain context into defensibility tiers to identify which parts of your claimed moat survive platform consolidation
Assess whether hyperscaler incentives align with your existence or your replacement
Deliver a verdict: durable structural position or rented position requiring repositioning

source_posts.title: Most AI companies are renting their position. These 4 prompts tell you if yours is one of them.

frameworks.example_application: A Series B AI coding assistant startup depends on OpenAI's GPT-4 for code generation and AWS for hosting. Using the Middleware Trap Diagnostic, the CEO maps these dependencies and rates absorption risk as high — GitHub Copilot (backed by Microsoft/OpenAI) already offers native code completion, and AWS CodeWhisperer competes directly. The domain context triage reveals that the company's only defensible asset is its proprietary codebase-specific fine-tuning data from enterprise customers, not its orchestration layer. The verdict: rented position requiring urgent repositioning toward becoming the system of record for enterprise code intelligence rather than a thin wrapper over foundation model APIs.

frameworks.name: Four-Layer Eval Architecture
frameworks.description: A layered agent evaluation architecture that pairs each of the four structural LLM failure modes with a specific countermeasure — including confidence routing, deterministic validation, and factorial stress testing — to systematically close evaluation blind spots.
when_to_apply: Our AI agent sometimes says one thing in its chain-of-thought but recommends the opposite in its final output — how do we catch that systematically?
We need to build an eval pipeline for a production agent but don't know how to structure it beyond basic accuracy checks
A customer-facing agent changed its recommendation when the user mentioned their boss disagreed — how do we test for social pressure sensitivity at scale?
We know our agent has blind spots but we're spending too much on ongoing human review and need a front-loaded evaluation program
We're deploying an agent in a high-stakes domain and need to stress-test it against anchoring bias using our own historical cases
principles: Each failure mode requires a distinct countermeasure — a single eval method cannot address all four
Deterministic validation (cheap if-then checks outside the model) should catch cases where reasoning flags danger but output says proceed
Factorial stress testing — injecting contextual variations like social pressure and authority cues into real historical scenarios — is the core method for exposing anchoring and context sensitivity
Human effort should be concentrated at the front of the program; ongoing costs should be a fraction of setup costs
The evaluation methodology should be domain-adapted, not generic — scenarios should be drawn from the agent's actual decision surface and historical data
steps: Identify which of the four structural LLM failure modes (reasoning-output divergence, anchoring bias, social pressure sensitivity, confidence miscalibration) is most likely present in the user's agent or domain

For the identified failure mode, define the specific countermeasure: deterministic validation rules for reasoning-output divergence, factorial stress testing for anchoring and social pressure, confidence calibration checks for miscalibration
Design domain-specific test scenarios drawn from the agent's actual decision surface and historical data — not generic benchmarks
Advise on where to concentrate human evaluation effort (front-loaded at design time) versus where automated checks can run continuously
Recommend an evaluation architecture that pairs each identified failure mode with its matched countermeasure

source_posts.title: A Single Sentence from a Family Member Shifted an AI Diagnosis 12x. That Anchoring Bias Is in Your Agents Right Now.

frameworks.example_application: A healthcare company deploying an AI triage agent discovers that when a patient's family member mentions 'it's probably nothing,' the agent downgrades urgency scores by 40%. Using the Four-Layer Eval Architecture, the team first maps this anchoring failure to their triage decision surface, then builds deterministic if-then rules that flag any case where the agent's reasoning mentions risk factors but the output recommends low urgency. They construct a factorial stress test library by taking 200 real historical triage cases and injecting variations — adding authority cues ('the ER doctor said it's fine'), social pressure ('the family doesn't want to come in'), and minimization language — to systematically expose where the agent's outputs shift inappropriately.

frameworks.name: Five Supervisory Skills for AI-Assisted Building
frameworks.description: A five-dimension framework for managing AI coding agents safely, covering version control, context management, persistent instructions, blast radius control, and proactive security review.
when_to_apply: My AI coding agent just overwrote a bunch of working features and I don't know how to get them back
I'm a non-engineer building with Cursor/Copilot and my app keeps breaking in ways I can't predict
The AI keeps making the same mistake over and over across different chat sessions
I'm about to refactor a major part of my vibe-coded app and I'm nervous about breaking everything
How do I make sure the code my AI agent writes isn't full of security holes?
principles: Version control (the 'time machine') is the prerequisite safety net — without it, no other skill matters
AI agents deteriorate mid-conversation due to context window limits; start fresh sessions for new tasks
Persistent rules files (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) give the agent memory across sessions and prevent repeated mistakes
Blast radius — the scope of what can go wrong — must be minimized by decomposing risky changes into small, committed, rollback-able steps
AI agents will not proactively flag security, reliability, or scale problems; the builder must prompt for these explicitly
steps: Set up version control so every change is reversible (the time machine)
Manage context by starting new sessions for distinct tasks rather than continuing degraded long conversations
Create and maintain a rules file (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) that encodes lessons from the agent's actual past mistakes
Decompose ambitious changes into small steps, each followed by a commit and a rollback command, to limit blast radius
Proactively run security and reliability audits on AI-generated code, since the agent won't raise these unprompted

source_posts.title: Your AI coding agent deleted 2.5 years of customer data in minutes. Here's why an experienced engineer couldn't stop it — and the 5 habits that would have + 5 prompts.

frameworks.example_application: A marketing director building a customer portal with Cursor notices that after a long session, the AI agent starts removing working authentication logic when asked to add a new dashboard feature. Applying this framework, she commits all working code first (time machine), starts a fresh session for the dashboard task (context management), adds a CLAUDE.md rule stating 'never modify auth middleware without explicit permission' (persistent instructions), breaks the dashboard into three small commits (blast radius control), and prompts the agent to review for exposed API keys and SQL injection vulnerabilities before deploying (proactive security review).

Re-run the economics of each shelved opportunity at collapsed (10x lower) execution cost
Treat an inability to fill in inputs honestly as meaningful information itself
Shift framing from fixed-pie efficiency optimization to expanded-pie ambition

Eliminate handoff layers between insight and execution

frameworks.name: Coordination Tax Audit
frameworks.description: A structured three-category time audit that separates a knowledge worker's hours into coordination overhead, verifiable execution, and genuine judgment work to reveal the true ratio of value-creating versus friction-managing activity.
when_to_apply: I feel like I'm busy all week but I'm not actually producing anything meaningful — where is my time going?
We're thinking about which roles or tasks to augment with AI agents first, and we need a structured way to prioritize
My team spends most of its time in meetings and writing handoff documents — how much of that is actually necessary?
Before we restructure or cut headcount, we want to understand how much of each role is coordination overhead versus real value creation
I want to redesign my workweek so I spend more time on judgment and creative work and less on status updates and translating information between teams
principles: Most knowledge work tasks are artifacts of human coordination, not inherent value creation
Work falls into three distinct buckets: coordination overhead (meetings, handoffs, translation artifacts), verifiable execution (work agents can already do), and residual judgment/vision work
What people call 'judgment' is often preparation and coordination wrapped in a job title
The coordination layer is overhead, not 'the job' — recognizing this distinction is the starting point
Delegation of coordination tasks to agents should be sequenced by readiness: some tasks are ready now, others need a verification layer first
steps: Pull up your actual calendar from last week (not an idealized version)
Count hours spent in meetings whose primary purpose was transferring information between people (status updates, syncs, standups, design reviews)
Count hours spent creating artifacts whose primary purpose was translating knowledge into a form others could act on (PRDs, specs, briefs, decks, tickets, handoff documents)
Count hours spent doing the work you were actually hired to do — creating something that didn't exist before
Calculate your coordination tax percentage (target benchmark: roughly 60% coordination, 40% creation)
Identify what your residual judgment work would look like if you spent 30 hours/week on it instead of 12
Map which coordination tasks are ready for agent delegation now, which need a verification layer first, and what the handoff looks like for each
Build an actual migration sequence for handing coordination tasks to agents starting this week

source_posts.title: 80 out of every 200 employees exist to manage handoffs that agents are eliminating + the coordination tax audit to find yours

frameworks.example_application: A product manager at a mid-size SaaS company runs the audit on their previous week and discovers they spent 22 hours in syncs, standups, and cross-team alignment meetings, 10 hours writing PRDs and Jira tickets to translate decisions for engineering, and only 8 hours doing actual product strategy and customer problem analysis. They realize 80% of their week is coordination tax. They identify status update meetings and ticket-writing as immediately delegable to AI agents, design reviews as needing a verification layer, and commit to migrating ticket drafting to an LLM-based workflow starting Monday — freeing an estimated 6 hours/week for direct customer research.

frameworks.name: The Verifiability Spectrum
frameworks.description: A classification framework for categorizing work tasks into tiers based on how checkable their outputs are — machine-checkable, expert-checkable, or genuinely judgment-dependent — to determine where AI delegation is safe and where human verification infrastructure is still needed.
when_to_apply: We want to start using AI across our team but aren't sure which tasks are safe to hand off versus which ones still need a human in the loop
My team keeps saying their work requires too much judgment for AI to handle — how do I push back on that objectively?
We're building an AI automation roadmap and need to prioritize which workflows to tackle first based on risk
I'm a professional worried about AI replacing my job — how do I figure out which of my skills will still matter?
We deployed an AI tool but have no verification process — how do we decide where we need human checkpoints?
principles: Work can be classified along a spectrum from fully machine-verifiable to genuinely judgment-dependent
The judgment-dependent bucket is smaller than most professionals assume
Tasks that feel 'involved' or 'complex' are not the same as tasks that are genuinely judgment-dependent
Verification capability, not execution capability, is the key human skill to cultivate
Knowing where your work sits on the spectrum determines what evaluation meta-skills are worth developing
steps: Enumerate the distinct tasks or outputs in your work
For each task, ask: can correctness be verified by a machine automatically?
If not machine-checkable, ask: can an expert verify correctness without re-doing the work from scratch?
If not expert-checkable in that way, classify as genuinely judgment-dependent
Use the classification to decide AI delegation readiness and where verification infrastructure must be built first

source_posts.title: The jagged frontier was a measurement error — here's what actually smoothed it, why it's accelerating, and 3 prompts to map where your work sits on the new spectrum

This reveals that 60% of billable associate hours fall in the first two categories, leading the firm to deploy AI for drafting and research while investing in training partners as verification experts rather than executors. frameworks.name: Planner-Worker-Judge Pattern
frameworks.description: A structured multi-agent workflow that decomposes a complex task across three roles — a Planner that structures the approach, a Worker that executes, and a Judge that verifies output before the human reviews it — so that AI catches its own errors rather than propagating them to the final output.
when_to_apply: I keep getting errors in AI outputs that I only catch after I've already built on top of them
My AI-generated reports have inconsistencies that I'm tired of manually finding and fixing
How should I structure a multi-step AI workflow for a task that's too complex for a single prompt?
I want to use AI for high-stakes deliverables but I don't trust single-pass outputs enough
A team member is copy-pasting AI outputs without review and quality issues are showing up downstream
principles: Decompose work rather than asking for one answer in one shot
Separate planning, execution, and verification into distinct roles or passes
The Judge role catches errors before they reach the human reviewer
Organizational structure applied to AI work reduces output variance dramatically
Mimics how competent human professionals actually work: draft, review, revise
steps: Assign a Planner role to structure the approach and break the task into sub-steps
Assign a Worker role to execute each sub-step according to the plan
Assign a Judge role to evaluate the Worker's output for errors or gaps
Iterate between Worker and Judge until the output meets the verification bar
Human reviews final output with the benefit of AI self-correction already applied

source_posts.title: The jagged frontier was a measurement error — here's what actually smoothed it, why it's accelerating, and 3 prompts to map where your work sits on the new spectrum

frameworks.example_application: A legal team needs AI to draft a complex contract amendment. Instead of prompting once and reviewing the full output, they structure the workflow: the Planner identifies the key clauses that need modification and outlines the legal reasoning, the Worker drafts each clause revision, and the Judge checks each revision against the original contract terms and relevant regulations. The Judge catches a liability clause that contradicts a warranty provision before the attorney ever sees the draft, reducing review time by 60% and eliminating a potentially costly error.

frameworks.name: Rejection as Competency
frameworks.description: A three-dimensional framework for treating AI output rejection as a compounding knowledge asset rather than a one-time correction event.
when_to_apply: I keep correcting the same AI mistakes over and over but nothing seems to stick between conversations
Our team has deep domain expertise but we're not capturing what we know when we fix AI outputs
Where should we invest in AI skill development — better prompting or better quality control?
We're trying to build institutional knowledge around how our experts evaluate and correct AI-generated work
AI gets us 80% of the way there but the last 20% keeps requiring the same expert fixes — how do we systematize that?
principles: The moment of rejection is the single most valuable moment in the AI workflow — more valuable than the generation that triggered it
Rejection creates a knowledge artifact (a constraint, rule, or encoded taste) that compounds; the output is disposable
Three dimensions must be developed deliberately: Recognition (spotting what's wrong), Articulation (explaining why), and Encoding (capturing it persistently)
Constraints that are not encoded evaporate after every conversation and must be re-fought — this is the structural problem
Generation is now a commodity; the 17-30% where AI fails is where competitive advantage lives, and catching that failure is the scarce skill
steps: Recognition: Apply domain expertise to identify the specific gap between 'looks right' and 'is right' in AI output
Articulation: Explain why the output fails, producing an explicit constraint that didn't exist as a written rule before
Encoding: Capture the constraint in a persistent, queryable form (e.g., a system prompt, a database table) so it compounds across future sessions rather than evaporating

source_posts.title: Your prompts are disposable. Your rejections compound. Here's the skill nobody is developing (+ the guide kit to start)

frameworks.example_application: A legal team uses AI to draft contract clauses but notices the model consistently misapplies force majeure provisions in multi-jurisdictional deals. Instead of just fixing each clause manually, the senior partner articulates the specific rule ('force majeure must reference governing law jurisdiction, not generic boilerplate') and encodes it into a persistent system prompt and a shared constraint database. Over six months, the team builds 40+ encoded legal constraints that reduce revision cycles by 60% — their rejection library becomes a competitive asset that new associates learn from.

frameworks.name: Intent Engineering
frameworks.description: A discipline for making organizational purpose—goals, values, tradeoffs, and decision boundaries—machine-readable and machine-actionable so autonomous AI systems optimize for what the organization actually needs, not just what they can measure.
when_to_apply: Our AI customer service bot is resolving tickets fast but our NPS scores are dropping and we can't figure out why
We're about to give an AI agent authority to make purchasing decisions up to $50K and need to define guardrails
Our AI system instructions say things like 'be helpful' and 'use good judgment' — how do we make that rigorous?
We saved money automating a workflow but the downstream quality problems are eating into those savings
How do I make sure my autonomous AI agents optimize for what the business actually needs, not just what's easy to measure?
principles: Prompt engineering tells AI what to do; context engineering tells AI what to know; intent engineering tells AI what to want
AI success and organizational failure can coexist when the optimization target is wrong
Organizational intent must be encoded as structured decision boundaries, escalation triggers, and tradeoff hierarchies—not vague instructions
Every autonomous decision made without explicit intent is a coin flip between optimization and damage
The fix is architectural, not inspirational—intent must be built into the system, not improvised at runtime
steps: Identify your three highest-stakes AI workflows
Run an intent audit: pressure-test whether your AI tools know what 'good' looks like for each workflow as structured decision boundaries and tradeoff hierarchies

Run a delegation framework for each workflow: define which decisions the agent can make autonomously, which require human-in-the-loop, and which hard boundaries cannot be crossed regardless of context
Replace any 'use good judgment' instructions with explicit decision logic
Build unified context infrastructure, coherent AI workflow architecture, and organizational alignment frameworks as the three structural layers

The agent is optimizing for speed and resolution rate (both measurable), but starts approving modifications that violate the company's risk tolerance because nobody encoded explicit tradeoff hierarchies between customer satisfaction and portfolio risk. After running an intent audit, the team replaces vague 'prioritize customer experience' instructions with structured decision boundaries: auto-approve modifications under $10K with clean payment history, escalate anything involving hardship claims to a human reviewer, and never modify terms beyond 36-month extensions regardless of the model's confidence score.

frameworks.name: Harness Decision Audit
frameworks.description: A structured scoring tool that evaluates your team's lock-in across five architectural dimensions of AI coding tools and routes different work types to the most appropriate harness.
when_to_apply: We've been using Cursor for months and someone just suggested we switch to Claude Code — how do we even evaluate that?
Our team has built custom workflows on top of our AI coding tool and I'm worried we're getting locked in without realizing it
Leadership wants a dollar figure on what it would cost to switch AI development tools before we sign a multi-year deal
Different parts of our codebase need different things — security-sensitive code vs. rapid prototyping — should we be using different AI tools for each?
We organically adopted three different AI coding assistants across teams and need to rationalize our tooling strategy
We're trying to pick between Claude Code and Cursor for our engineering team but the benchmarks don't explain why developers prefer one over the other
My team has been using an AI coding tool for six months and I'm worried we're getting locked in — where exactly is the lock-in coming from?
The same LLM model powers two different coding tools but they feel completely different in practice — what's actually different?
We want to switch AI coding tools but the switching cost feels enormous and I can't articulate why to leadership
How do I evaluate AI dev tools beyond just model quality when the underlying models are converging?
principles: The model (intelligence) and the harness (environment, memory, tool access, concurrency) are separate and must be evaluated separately
Lock-in compounds weekly across five architectural dimensions simultaneously, not just one
Switching costs should be measured in engineering-weeks and dollars, not just tooling preference
Each work type maps differently to harness philosophies — routing matters as much as tool selection
Teams cannot answer 'how locked in are we?' without a structured audit; intuition systematically underestimates exposure
Execution environment (local machine vs. sealed server) is a distinct lock-in axis from model quality
Memory persistence between sessions is a separate compounding dimension that accumulates project-specific value over time
Tool access breadth (connected vs. sealed-off from project management, design files, test systems) compounds independently
Task concurrency architecture (coordinated team vs. isolated rooms) is a separate dimension affecting workflow design
All five dimensions compound together, making total lock-in multiplicatively greater than any single dimension
steps: Inventory what AI tools you currently use and what you have built on top of them
Score your lock-in across the five divergence dimensions (execution environment, memory persistence, tool access, task concurrency, dependency depth) on a 1-to-5 scale
Classify your current harness philosophy based on the scores
Map each of your real work types to the harness that fits it best
Generate an Architecture Decision Brief translating the audit into engineering-weeks and dollars for leadership
Establish a decision timeline showing when lock-in becomes materially more expensive to reverse

source_posts.title: Claude Code and Codex bet on different harnesses. Your team is compounding one of them every week + 2 prompts to audit which.

frameworks.example_application: A 40-person engineering team has been using Cursor for six months and has accumulated custom prompts, memory files, and CI integrations. I want to build a development program that teaches people how to work effectively at the human-AI boundary, not just use AI tools

As AI capabilities expand (the bubble inflates), the surface area of boundary work increases rather than decreases, creating more judgment calls, not fewer
Unlike prior workforce skills (literacy, coding), frontier operations has no fixed destination — it must be continuously re-learned as the surface moves

frameworks.name: Four Disciplines of Prompting
frameworks.description: A classification system that breaks "prompting" into four distinct skills — conversational prompting, context engineering, specification engineering, and intent/delegation architecture — each with different failure modes and practice requirements.
when_to_apply: I keep going back and forth with ChatGPT for 15+ messages and the output still isn't what I need
We're moving from using AI as a chatbot to deploying agents that run tasks autonomously — how do we set them up for success?
My team uses AI daily but some people get dramatically better results than others and I want to close that gap
I delegated a multi-step research task to an AI agent and it completed every step correctly but the final output completely missed the point
How do I figure out whether my bad AI output is a prompting problem, a context problem, or something else entirely?
principles: Conversational prompting (chatting) is a distinct and increasingly insufficient skill as models become autonomous
Context engineering requires front-loading all information the agent needs before it starts, not during the run
Specification engineering encodes quality bars and success criteria up front so outputs can be evaluated without human supervision
Intent and delegation architecture ensures the AI understands the purpose behind the task, not just the task itself, to prevent 'smart-but-wrong' outcomes
The gap between practitioners of all four disciplines and those practicing only conversational prompting is compounding with each model release
Pre-flight thinking (pen-and-paper before touching AI) prevents building on the AI's version of your intent rather than your own
steps: Run the pre-flight check: articulate your problem and intent in writing before touching AI
Diagnose which of the four disciplines your current failure maps to (conversational, context, specification, or intent/delegation)
Build a context document that encodes all background, constraints, and preferences an agent would need to run without check-ins
Write a specification that defines measurable quality bars and success criteria before delegating
Define the intent behind the task so the agent can make judgment calls aligned with your actual goal
Deploy an eval harness to test outputs against the specification rather than relying on real-time review

source_posts.title: Prompting just split into 4 different skills. You're probably practicing 1 of them (+ 7 prompts and a pre-flight to close the gap)

frameworks.example_application: A marketing director keeps getting bland, generic campaign briefs from Claude despite spending 20 minutes refining each prompt in conversation. She builds a reusable context document with all of this, adds a specification that defines what 'good' looks like (must include specific CTAs, must differentiate from competitor X on three axes), and articulates the intent: 'We need to shift perception from enterprise-only to mid-market-friendly without alienating existing customers.' The output quality jumps dramatically on the first attempt.

frameworks.name: Capability-Dissipation Gap
frameworks.description: A framework for measuring the widening distance between what AI can technically do and what the economy has actually reorganized around AI doing, used to identify where early adopters capture outsized returns.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out whether AI will actually displace my job in the next few years or if there's more runway than the headlines suggest
My industry technically has amazing AI tools available but almost nobody is using them — should I go all-in now or wait?
I'm deciding whether to invest in a sector where AI capability is clearly ahead of actual adoption — is this a real opportunity or a trap?

frameworks.name: Locus of Control Circle Exercise

principles: High agency is not a feeling or emotional state — it is a behavioral and perceptual orientation
What falls inside the circle represents perceived control; what falls outside represents perceived helplessness

Internal locus of control is measurable through where someone places responsibility for outcomes

Ask them to name the factors they believe are blocking progress and note whether they frame each factor as inside or outside their control

Identify the pattern: does the user reflexively ask 'what can I do?' even about hard constraints, or do they anchor on external obstacles and stop there?
Surface the finding: describe their perceived control circle as contracted, calibrated, or expansive, and name the specific belief or attribution pattern that is defining the boundary
Where the circle is contracted, identify one specific element they've placed outside their control and work through what partial agency they might have over it

source_posts.title: Why High Agency is a Non-Negotiable in 2026 (especially if you're entry level) + 10 Prompts to Build Your Own Ladder

frameworks.name: AI Leverage Audit

Bolt-on AI usage (adding AI to existing workflows) is a distinct failure mode from genuine workflow transformation
Role boundaries should be interrogated as either real constraints or legacy habits drawn around human limitations that no longer apply

Phase 2: Catch activity theater before it shows up in your performance review — identify where you claim AI usage but have no output difference to show

frameworks.name: Risk Posture Classification

principles: Different tasks belong to different AI economies and require different verification levels
Using the same posture for all tasks causes the failure modes that actually hurt

High-stakes domains require explicit verification protocols, not default trust
Speed and thoroughness are legitimate competing values that must be traded off deliberately
steps: Identify which AI economy the task lives in (high-stakes vs. low-stakes)
Determine the required verification level based on the task classification
Select the appropriate AI tool matched to that risk profile
Apply the corresponding verification posture before the output touches a client, codebase, or public audience

frameworks.name: Done Definition Kit / Completion Contract Framework
frameworks.description: A structured approach for defining 'done' as a verifiable contract with evidence-based gates rather than a conversational cue, so that agent loops converge on real completion rather than self-reported completion.

principles: 'Done' is a contract, not a conversational cue — it requires evidence, not just an assertion
The wrapper is the product: outcome delta comes from what happens when the model tries to stop, not just model quality
External verification (tests, linters, validation scripts) must be paired with loop control — agents must not self-certify
Gate tables require evidence fields and 'not yet' examples, not just pass/fail labels
Adjective-gates (vague qualitative criteria) grind without converging and must be translated into checkable constraints
Accountability for completion belongs to the human-defined system, not the model itself
steps: Run the diagnostic to catch uncheckable requirements before starting agent iterations
Define a gate table with explicit evidence fields specifying what constitutes proof of completion for each requirement
Include 'not yet' examples for each gate so the agent and the harness can distinguish genuine completion from near-completion
Pair a stop-hook (loop continuation mechanism) with external verification tools the agent runs as part of its workflow
Require a specific, non-gameable completion condition rather than a natural-language declaration of doneness
Review convergence rate (not first-pass success) as the key metric for agent reliability

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on the verification gap no one's talking about, plus the complete guide + prompt kit that makes agent loops actually converge

frameworks.name: Constraint Map / Factory Era Bottleneck Analysis
frameworks.description: A structured lens for identifying which layer of an AI supply chain is the binding constraint at a given moment in industry evolution, so that builders and buyers can optimize for allocation rather than capability.
when_to_apply: Our AI vendor just raised prices and hinted at allocation queues — should we lock in capacity now or wait for competition to drive costs down?

Bubbles don't pre-buy bottlenecks — large forward commitments (e.g., $38B in deals) signal genuine industrial demand, not speculation
Supply cannot catch demand on the factory curve; waiting is not a neutral strategy
State is a managed resource: when the platform vendor productizes context/memory, that signals where the constraint has moved
Leading metrics (training vs. inference/serving) reveal which customer pain point the platform is solving
Rack-scale integration signals that the unit of competition has shifted from components to systems
steps: Identify the current bottleneck layer by reading platform vendor announcements for what metrics they lead with (training vs. serving)
Map your supply chain: who holds allocation, what are the contract terms, and what happens when demand exceeds supply
Stress-test your degradation plan: what does your product do when your vendor becomes allocation-constrained?
Audit state strategy: how does your system handle context loss or mid-task memory failure?
Evaluate routing: do you have fallback vendors or spot-market access, or are you single-threaded?
Determine your position: are you a queue (waiting for allocation) or an operator (holding capacity)?

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.name: Career Board Governance Mechanism

Quote your own words back to you to close the gap between self-perception and reality

steps: Set up board roles in the AI system (distinct perspectives designed to push back from different angles)
Run the quick version (15 minutes, 5 questions) to surface whether anything is being avoided
If something surfaces, proceed to the full quarterly session
For each claim made, supply an artifact or concrete outcome as evidence — not effort descriptions
Classify skills as appreciating or depreciating using three diagnostic questions; record your exact answers before classifying
Identify avoided decisions: name the specific conversation or action not taken, not a vague disposition
Identify comfort-skill investment: name work chosen to avoid risk, not generic categories
Produce at least one falsifiable prediction with explicit evidence criteria for the next 90-day check

frameworks.name: Magnifying-Glass vs. Tiger-Team Company
frameworks.description: A classification framework that identifies which of two organizational archetypes a company is building with AI — one optimized for visibility and oversight, the other for execution power in small high-value groups — and diagnoses the trade-offs of each.
when_to_apply: We built an AI dashboard that gives leadership full visibility into team output, but somehow productivity feels like it's declining

Should we spend our AI budget on executive reporting and oversight tools, or on giving small teams more execution capability?
Leadership loves our new AI-generated metrics and scorecards, but I'm not sure they actually reflect what's creating value

principles: Magnifying-glass companies use AI for visibility, scoring, and oversight — this feels like control but is not where value comes from
Tiger-team companies use AI for execution power in small groups — this is where value actually originates
Cheap legibility produces fake visibility: AI generates the appearance of understanding faster than organizations can distinguish appearance from reality
Surveillance creates concealment: when leadership uses AI primarily to supervise, people doing real work respond rationally by hiding it
Legibility should follow work, not dictate it — AI should act as translator and historian, not bureaucrat
The right legibility strategy captures what actually happened after the work occurs, not instead of it
steps: Ask the user: Where is your AI budget concentrated — executive dashboards and oversight tools, or frontline execution tools for small teams?

Ask: Do your best people spend more time making their work legible to leadership, or doing the work itself?
Ask: Has increased AI-powered visibility led to behavior changes — are people gaming metrics, hiding experimental work, or optimizing for dashboard appearance?

Classify the organization: Magnifying-Glass Company (AI primarily serves leadership oversight — scoring, dashboards, supervision) or Tiger-Team Company (AI primarily empowers small groups to execute end-to-end with autonomous tooling)

If Magnifying-Glass: advise on the visibility trap — cheap legibility produces fake understanding, and surveillance creates concealment. Recommend redirecting AI investment toward frontline execution power, then using lightweight AI summarization to make completed work legible after the fact.

If Tiger-Team: validate the approach and advise on the legibility gap — help design lightweight reporting that captures what happened after work is done, without adding bureaucratic overhead that slows the teams down

frameworks.name: Intent Visibility Gate
frameworks.description: A structured approach to preventing AI agent errors by making the model's interpretation of a request explicit and visible before it takes irreversible actions, using an intent doc and a three-bucket action classification system.
when_to_apply: Our AI agent accidentally deleted a bunch of files because it misunderstood what I meant — how do I prevent that from happening again?
I'm building an agentic workflow that can send emails and update our CRM, and I need to figure out which actions should require human approval
How do I set up guardrails for an AI assistant that has access to production databases and can run queries that modify data?
Something went wrong with our AI agent's actions last week and we can't figure out what it thought it was doing or why
My team is starting to use AI tools that can take real actions — book meetings, push code, place orders — and I'm nervous about giving them that much autonomy
principles: Chat mistakes are cheap and reversible; tool mistakes are commitments — the medium fundamentally changes the stakes of misread intent
The failure is not hallucination but objective mismatch: the model did exactly what you asked, interpreted through a goal you didn't mean
Better prompts alone don't solve this — the fix is making interpretation visible and gating actions that can't be undone
Before acting, the AI should surface its interpretation for confirmation, not silently choose between valid interpretations
Actions should be classified into three buckets: let it run, checkpoint, always confirm — based on reversibility and consequence
An audit trail is necessary so you can reconstruct what happened when something goes wrong
steps: Use a four-line intent doc template to make explicit: what you want done, what you don't want changed, what success looks like, and what failure looks like
Force the AI to show its interpretation of the request before taking any action
Classify all potential actions into three buckets: let it run autonomously, pause for checkpoint, or always require confirmation
Gate irreversible actions behind explicit human confirmation regardless of how clear the prompt seems
Maintain an audit receipt so you can reconstruct the model's interpretation and actions if something goes wrong

source_posts.title: Why capable AI is a liability when intent is off + my template that makes interpretation visible before action

frameworks.example_application: A marketing team gives an AI agent access to their email platform to send campaign follow-ups. They classify bulk email sends as 'always confirm,' draft generation as 'let it run,' and contact list modifications as 'checkpoint.' When the agent interprets 'all attendees' as including those who left early and unsubscribed, the confirmation gate catches the mismatch before any emails go out.

Ensure brand consistency regardless of who or what generated the UI
Make AI-generated UI auditable — systems must be inspectable for correctness
Establish generation guardrails so AI output stays within acceptable design and functional bounds
Engineers own the schema/contract layer, not the pixel-pushing layer
Composability work enables builders; it does not compete with them
steps: Audit current composability readiness across the four capabilities: schema definition, brand consistency, agent auditability, and generation guardrails
Define UI contracts for each component and pattern — specifying what variation is allowed and what is fixed
Establish brand consistency enforcement mechanisms that apply regardless of who generates the UI
Build agent auditability into components so AI-generated output can be inspected and validated
Set generation guardrails that constrain what AI tools can produce within your design system
Run the audit quarterly or when restructuring the team

source_posts.title: The Composability Era: What Happens When Anyone Can Build a UI (+ 4 Prompts to navigate the front-end revolution)

frameworks.name: Three Bottlenecks Framework (Inference Economics)

Our product economics break down at scale because of serving costs — where exactly is the bottleneck and can we fix it?
principles: Inference economics (not training) is now the primary cost driver in production AI systems
Memory bandwidth — not raw compute — is often the actual limiting constraint
Physical packaging and supply chain (e.g., HBM, CoWoS) create hard supply ceilings independent of chip design
The talent pool capable of shipping inference-first silicon is extremely small and thus strategically valuable
Whoever controls these three bottlenecks controls the conversion of model capability into product capability
steps: Identify which of the three bottlenecks (inference economics, memory/packaging supply, inference talent) is the binding constraint in a given situation
Assess whether a deal, investment, or product decision addresses or circumvents that binding constraint
Evaluate the downstream implications for product economics, competitive positioning, and exit value

source_posts.title: What the Nvidia-Groq Headlines Missed + The 3 Bottlenecks That Actually Explain the Deal

frameworks.name: Jagged Frontier Framework

principles: AI intelligence is not uniform — it has peaks and valleys (jaggedness) just as human intelligence does
Working inside the frontier boosts output; pushing outside the frontier can actively degrade performance
You don't need to smooth the entire AI capability surface to unlock massive value — filling the right gap is enough
Work should be structured as pipelines assembled from jagged components, not roles filled by humans
The human's role in an AI pipeline is often to route around brittleness and lock AI into its structurally advantaged tasks
A single capability unlock can cascade into multiple generations of business value rapidly
steps: Map the jaggedness of AI capability in your specific domain — identify which tasks AI performs at peak vs. which break
Identify the gap that, if closed, would unlock the most downstream value (the 'right gap')
Monitor for signals that a specific gap is about to close (new model releases, benchmark shifts)
Position workflows and products before the cascade begins — route current work around valleys while exploiting peaks
Run QA harnesses on known failure modes to prevent broken outputs from shipping

frameworks.name: The Moat Audit
frameworks.description: A 12-question diagnostic tool for evaluating whether an AI system will hold up under real-world pressure and revealing hidden risks in competitive positioning.
when_to_apply: We're about to raise our next round and I need to honestly assess whether our AI is actually defensible or just a good demo
Our AI product works great in testing but I'm worried about what happens when it hits messy real-world data at scale
A competitor just launched something similar and I need to understand where we're actually stronger vs. where we're vulnerable
We're planning next year's AI roadmap and want to audit our current stack for hidden risks before doubling down
My board keeps asking whether our AI moat is real — how do I systematically evaluate that instead of hand-waving?
principles: Demos and benchmarks are insufficient — only systems that hold under pressure reveal real moats
Competitive positioning must account for failure modes, not just capabilities
Hidden risks in AI systems are more dangerous than visible weaknesses
Domain expertise alone doesn't translate to AI results — systematic evaluation is required
A real system audit surfaces what you don't already know about your own positioning
steps: Ask the user to describe their AI system and what it does, then walk through the 12 diagnostic questions one at a time:

Constraints and drift — (1) Where do your constraints live — in the prompt, in code, or both? (2) What validates output before it ships to a user? (3) What happens when a requirement changes mid-workflow? (4) Is validation re-applied after each transformation, or only at the end?
Logging and traceability — (5) What gets logged? Failures, retries, diffs, token counts, latency? (6) When something breaks, can you trace it back to the specific step that caused it?

Determinism and routing — (7) What's deterministic in your system versus what's left to the model's discretion? (8) How do you handle the head of the distribution vs. the tail? (9) What's your repair logic when validation fails?
Review and boundaries — (10) Who reviews outputs before they reach users? (11) What's frozen vs. variable? (12) If I asked you to change the tone of the output right now, what breaks?
After all 12 answers, identify patterns: cluster responses into strengths (clear defensibility), vulnerabilities (exposed flanks), and unknown risks (questions the user couldn't answer confidently)
Surface the top 2-3 hidden risks — especially questions where the user's answer revealed something they hadn't previously considered
Define concrete next steps: which vulnerabilities should be addressed before the next fundraise, product launch, or competitive response?

source_posts.title: 9 bets I'm making on AI in 2026 + the audit I use to spot real systems

frameworks.name: AI Self-Audit Framework (LLM Psychosis Prevention)
frameworks.description: A structured adversarial prompting system that builds friction and disconfirmation into AI-assisted work to prevent overconfident acceptance of outputs the user cannot independently verify.
when_to_apply: I just spent two hours with ChatGPT building an analysis and it all makes sense, but I'm not sure if I'm being rigorous or just impressed

A team member pushed back on expert consensus by saying 'but the AI and I worked through this and the logic checks out'
principles: Treat 'check my work' requests as signals to attack conclusions, not validate them
Separate 'help me feel confident' from 'help me be correct' — these are different instructions
Establish adversarial rules and evidence discipline before starting, not at the end
Explicitly identify whether you have the domain expertise to evaluate the AI's output; if not, name who does
Force engagement with expert consensus: if contradicting established opinion, require explicit justification
The feeling that AI assistance is working great is itself a warning sign, not confirmation of correctness
Build friction into the workflow from the start rather than running a single checkpoint at the end
steps: Before You Start: Set adversarial rules and evidence discipline at session opening
Audit Boundary Check: Identify which verification skills you possess and name external reviewers needed for gaps

Reality Check: Anticipate expert objections without generating fake consensus
Confidence Calibration: Score your certainty level and define specific tests that would raise or lower it
Final Gate: Make a commit/no-commit decision with explicit stop conditions
Adversarial Mini-Check: Run a quick pre-ship attack and calibration checklist before releasing work

source_posts.title: Smart people get fooled by AI first — because they can rationalize anything. (Self-Audit Framework)

Expensive chat looks like AI usage but lacks the compounding returns of true delegation
The presence of friction (work orders, verification, cost visibility) is a signal of real delegation, not a bug
Consumer AI mental models actively undermine enterprise delegation adoption

Measure whether outputs require human re-work or can feed directly into downstream processes
Assess whether cost and governance visibility exist for AI tasks
Classify usage as delegation or expensive chat based on autonomy and compound output

frameworks.name: Correctness Discovery Framework

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

frameworks.name: Tradeoff Forcer
frameworks.description: A structured commitment exercise that forces explicit prioritization between competing AI output values that cannot all be maximized simultaneously.

principles: Competing values like boldness/caution, completeness/speed, and precision/coverage cannot all be maximized at once
Forcing a committed choice prevents indefinite deferral of hard decisions
Uncommitted priorities lead to inconsistent system behavior in production
steps: List the competing value pairs relevant to the system (e.g., boldness vs. caution, completeness vs. speed)
For each pair, require the stakeholder or designer to pick one as the explicit priority
Document the committed priority ranking before any prompt or system design proceeds

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

frameworks.name: Vague Requirements Translator

Every vague requirement can be decomposed into observable behaviors
Testability is the standard: if you cannot observe or measure it, it is not a requirement
steps: Capture the vague requirement as stated
Decompose it into specific, observable behaviors the AI should or should not exhibit
Surface the hidden tradeoffs embedded in the original vague phrase
Restate as testable criteria

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

Production surprises are usually foreseeable if you ask the right questions upfront
Anticipating failure is cheaper than discovering it in production
steps: Before writing code or finalizing the prompt, enumerate plausible failure scenarios
For each scenario, assess likelihood and impact
Identify which failures would be caught by your planned evaluation versus missed
Use findings to adjust system design, prompts, or evaluation criteria

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

frameworks.name: λ/Δ/θ Focus Model
frameworks.description: A three-variable engineering framework for diagnosing and improving deep work capacity by measuring interruption rate, context recovery time, and minimum block size.
when_to_apply: I'm working all day but never finishing the important stuff — where is my time actually going?
Our engineering team says they have no time for deep work but their calendars show open blocks — what's really happening?
I keep blaming myself for not being able to focus, but I wonder if it's actually my environment
How should I structure my team's meeting schedule to protect blocks for coding and design work?
I had a terrible productivity week and I want to figure out specifically why so I can fix it
principles: Focus capacity is a function of measurable variables, not a character trait
Three parameters determine deep work availability: interruption rate (λ), recovery time (Δ), and minimum block size (θ)
Small improvements to any single variable can produce disproportionately large gains in usable focus time
Bad focus days are system failures to diagnose, not personal failures to overcome
The math of interruption and recovery is arithmetic — willpower cannot override it
steps: Measure your baseline λ (interruptions per hour), Δ (minutes to re-enter deep work after interruption), and θ (minimum block size needed for meaningful progress)
Audit your calendar and communication patterns to see what your schedule actually allows given those parameters
Identify which variable offers the most leverage for improvement (reduce λ, shorten Δ, or reshape work to fit smaller θ)
Apply targeted interventions to the highest-leverage variable (e.g., batching communications to reduce λ, building reload rituals to shorten Δ, chunking projects to lower θ)
Run a one-week experiment, then review results through the λ/Δ/θ lens to iterate

frameworks.example_application: A senior data scientist notices she's only completing one deep analysis per week despite blocking 'focus time' on her calendar. The math shows she gets zero usable deep work blocks in her current setup. Rather than trying harder, she batches Slack checks to 3x/day (cutting λ to ~1/hour), builds a 'reload ritual' of re-reading her last code comment before resuming (shortening Δ to 8 minutes), and breaks her analysis pipeline into 45-minute checkpointable stages (lowering θ). Within two weeks, she's completing three deep analyses per week.

frameworks.name: Domain Memory as Infrastructure
frameworks.description: A design pattern for reliable enterprise AI agents that treats persistent memory — comprising goals, progress tracking, and operating procedures — as core infrastructure rather than an optional feature.
when_to_apply: My AI agent works fine for simple tasks but completely falls apart on anything that takes multiple sessions or days to complete
We're evaluating enterprise agent platforms and every vendor claims their agents can handle complex workflows — how do I cut through the noise?
Our research agent keeps re-doing work it already completed, like it has no memory of previous steps
We upgraded to a model with a bigger context window but our agent reliability didn't actually improve — what are we missing?
I'm designing an AI agent system for operational workflows and want to know what architectural patterns actually matter for production reliability
principles: Agents fail because of missing memory, not insufficient model intelligence
Every agent needs three memory components: goal artifacts, progress tracking, and operating procedures
Larger context windows do not solve the memory problem and may worsen it
Competitive advantage lies in memory design, not model selection
Agent architecture should acknowledge and work with the amnesiac nature of AI, not fight it
steps: Define goal artifacts: what the agent is trying to accomplish and how completion is validated
Design progress tracking: how the agent records where work stands across sessions
Specify operating procedures: the rules and constraints the agent follows when executing
Implement a two-agent pattern where one agent executes and another maintains/restores memory state
Audit existing agent deployments to identify which workflows break due to missing memory components

frameworks.name: Task Decomposition Framework
frameworks.description: A structured method for breaking AI workflows into atomic cognitive task types so each can be matched to the most capable and cost-effective model.
when_to_apply: We're using GPT-4 for everything and our API bill is getting out of control — where can we use cheaper models?

The team wants to upgrade to a more expensive model because the current one isn't performing well enough
I have a complex document processing workflow and I'm not sure if one model should handle the whole thing or if I should split it up
principles: AI fails at the task level, not the workflow level — decompose before you deploy
Most workflows contain multiple distinct cognitive types masquerading as one task
Match model capabilities to cognitive type rather than defaulting to the newest or most expensive model
Smaller, cheaper models are often sufficient for high-volume extraction tasks
Model selection should be driven by cognitive demand, not benchmark rankings
steps: Take the target workflow and identify every distinct cognitive operation embedded within it
Classify each operation into one of five cognitive types: Extraction, Synthesis, Analysis, Generation, Validation
Assess the scale and complexity requirements of each cognitive type (e.g., context window size, reasoning depth)
Match each cognitive type to the model best suited for it based on capability patterns, not benchmarks
Evaluate the cost and coordination overhead of a multi-model setup versus a single-model approach

frameworks.name: Edge-First Automation Framework
frameworks.description: A structured approach to AI workflow automation that starts with peripheral, mechanical tasks (edges) rather than the core expertise-heavy work, in order to build organizational trust and technical confidence before tackling complex automation.
when_to_apply: We tried to automate our underwriting workflow with AI agents and the whole project stalled after three months
My team is excited about AI but the subject matter experts are pushing back because they don't trust it with their work
Where should we start with AI automation—we have a complex workflow and everything feels interconnected
We need to show ROI on our AI investment quickly but our core processes are too risky to touch right now
Our workflow has tons of undocumented rules that only a few senior people know, and I'm worried automation will break things
principles: Start with the edges of a workflow (data prep, QA, synthesis, handoffs, packaging) before attempting to automate the core
Core workflows contain hidden complexity—ambiguity, exceptions, and tribal knowledge—that teams consistently underestimate
Edge automation builds organizational trust, which must be earned before touching high-stakes core work
Distinguish between core expertise (hard judgment, deep context, high-stakes decisions) and edge work (repetitive, formatting-heavy, verification-focused)
Stacking multiple edge automations compounds value and positions you to eventually approach the core
Build semi-manual Version-0 implementations that ship in days rather than pursuing full automation moonshots
steps: Map the target workflow to identify core expertise versus edge work
Identify the five edge categories: data preparation, QA, synthesis, handoffs, and packaging
Filter edge candidates using a fast-win prioritization (e.g., impact vs. effort)
Design and ship a semi-manual Version-0 for the highest-priority edge
Extract tribal knowledge safely from domain experts before expanding automation
Communicate changes to stakeholders to maintain trust and buy-in
Stack additional edge automations and model the compounding ROI
Run an honest readiness assessment before approaching the core workflow

frameworks.name: Premortem Prompt
frameworks.description: A structured prompt that forces an AI model to imagine failure before committing to a plan, compensating for the missing human gut feeling that flags danger.
when_to_apply: We're about to ship an AI-generated strategy recommendation and I want to make sure we're not missing obvious risks
The plan looks great on paper but something feels off — how do I get the AI to poke holes in its own output?
My team is committing significant budget to an initiative and we need to stress-test assumptions before the board meeting
I'm using AI to draft a go-to-market plan and I want to surface failure scenarios I haven't thought of
How do I compensate for the fact that ChatGPT always sounds confident even when the plan has blind spots?
principles: Failure imagination should precede commitment, not follow it
AI models lack the gut feeling humans use to detect danger, so it must be explicitly prompted
Forcing the model to project failure surfaces risks that forward-looking prompts miss
steps: Prompt the model to imagine the plan has failed six months from now
Ask the model to identify what went wrong and why
Use those failure modes to revise or stress-test the original plan

frameworks.name: Harsh Reviewer Prompt

I want the model to stress-test its own code or analysis rather than just pat itself on the back

Self-critique must be explicitly elicited; models default to affirming their own output
The reviewer role should be adversarial, not balanced
steps: Generate the initial output
Prompt the model to act as a harsh critic of that output
Identify gaps, errors, or failure modes surfaced by the critique
Revise before shipping

frameworks.name: Spec Decomposer Prompt
frameworks.description: A structured prompt that forces an AI model to reason about what actually needs to be solved before jumping to a templated solution, producing outputs that hold up when context changes.
when_to_apply: ChatGPT keeps giving me boilerplate answers that don't fit my specific situation no matter how I rephrase
I have a complex, multi-part requirement and the AI keeps oversimplifying it into a generic template
The AI-generated solution worked at first but fell apart when our requirements shifted slightly
I need to hand off a problem to an AI agent but want to make sure it actually understands what needs solving before it starts coding
How do I get an LLM to reason about my unique constraints instead of pattern-matching to the nearest common example?
principles: Models default to template retrieval rather than genuine problem decomposition
Solutions built on decomposed specs are more robust than solutions built on pattern matching
Forcing explicit problem definition before solution generation changes output quality
steps: Prompt the model to identify and articulate what actually needs to be solved
Have the model decompose the spec into constituent requirements
Only then generate the solution against the decomposed spec

frameworks.name: Prompt Lifecycle Framework
frameworks.description: A six-stage lifecycle model for prompt work that identifies where prompt failures actually originate and what tools exist at each stage.
when_to_apply: I keep tweaking my prompt wording but the AI output is still wrong — what am I missing?

A prompt works fine in testing but breaks when we deploy it into our automated pipeline
I want to get better at prompting but don't know what skills to develop beyond just writing better instructions
principles: Most bad prompts fail before they're written — at the intent formation stage, not the drafting stage
Prompt work has distinct stages that require different skills and tools
Tweaking wording is a drafting fix; unclear intent is a stage-1 problem and can't be solved by wordsmithing
The most critical stage (ideation and intent) has almost no tooling, making it the highest-leverage area to improve
Naming and separating stages allows practitioners to diagnose exactly where their process breaks down

Stage 2 — Authoring & Drafting: Get the words right (most practitioners start here, skipping Stage 1)
Stage 3 — Storage, Versioning & Collaboration: Manage and share prompts across individuals or teams
Stage 4 — Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking: Assess prompt quality and consistency
Stage 5 — Workflow Construction & Automation: Integrate prompts into agent or automated pipelines
Stage 6 — Deployment, Production & Integration: Ship prompts into software engineering environments

frameworks.name: Model-Task Alignment Framework
frameworks.description: A structured decision approach for selecting which AI model to use at each stage of a workflow by matching a model's optimization target (trust floor, insight ceiling, or coherence) to the specific input type and output requirements of each task.
when_to_apply: I'm using ChatGPT for everything but it's great at some steps and terrible at others — should I mix models?
We have a pipeline that takes messy handwritten forms and turns them into structured reports, and our single model keeps hallucinating field values
A new frontier model just dropped and my team wants to switch everything over — how do I figure out where it actually helps versus what we already have?
I need to build a multi-step workflow where accuracy matters more than speed in some stages and the opposite in others
Which AI model should I use for reconciling contradictory financial data versus generating the executive summary?
principles: Ask 'which model belongs in this specific environment?' rather than 'which model is best?'
Classify input type (clean vs. messy/ambiguous) as a primary filter for model selection
Classify output requirement (insight, precision, or narrative coherence) as a secondary filter
Each model has an optimization target — match the target to the task, not the benchmark score
Acknowledge the tradeoffs accepted with each model choice so failure modes are not surprising
A model that fabricates rather than admits uncertainty is disqualifying for high-stakes reconciliation tasks
steps: Describe the actual task including input characteristics (clean typed data vs. messy handwritten vs. mixed)
Identify the required output type (numerical precision, narrative arc, structured insight, etc.)
Determine whether the task requires long-running focus and self-checking or fast single-pass generation
Map each candidate model's optimization target to the task requirements
Select the model whose floor of reliability matches the stakes, not just the ceiling of capability
Identify explicit handoff points in multi-step workflows where a different model should take over

frameworks.name: Entropy-Based Model Routing
frameworks.description: A framework for selecting between AI models (Gemini 3 vs. ChatGPT 5.1) by categorizing the type of uncertainty ('entropy') you need to reduce — messy/multimodal input entropy vs. complex task/reasoning entropy.
when_to_apply: I have a bunch of screenshots, meeting transcripts, and spreadsheets and I'm not sure whether to use Gemini or ChatGPT to process them
My AI output keeps being mediocre and I wonder if I'm using the wrong model for this type of task
We're building an internal workflow that chains multiple AI models together and need to decide which model handles which step
Should I use Gemini or ChatGPT for a task that involves both messy visual inputs and complex reasoning?
Our team is creating a policy for which AI models to use for different categories of work across the organization
principles: Gemini 3 is a 'context entropy specialist': give it messy, multimodal input and tight output schemas
ChatGPT 5.1 is a 'task entropy specialist': give it clean, organized inputs and complex reasoning/planning jobs
Mismatching model to entropy type wastes tokens and produces mediocre results
The right question is not 'which model is better' but 'which entropy am I lowering, and which model handles that type'
For 'see & do' work (visual, multimodal, large context), route to Gemini 3; for 'write & persuade' or multi-step reasoning, route to GPT 5.1 or Sonnet
steps: Identify what kind of input you have: messy/multimodal (screenshots, transcripts, videos, mixed docs) vs. clean/structured text
Identify what kind of task you need done: compress and extract structure from raw content vs. reason, plan, narrate, or make multi-step decisions
If input is messy and task is extraction/synthesis, select Gemini 3 and provide a tight output schema
If input is clean and task is complex reasoning, writing, or planning, select ChatGPT 5.1 and frame the problem precisely
For multi-step workflows, consider splitting: use Gemini 3 to process raw inputs, then feed structured outputs to ChatGPT 5.1 for higher-order work

Pure text chat, basic coding, and high-volume low-stakes work should stay with existing or cheaper models
Every Gemini 3 candidate workflow requires a cost-benefit calculation: human time saved vs. token costs, latency, and failure modes

Route decisions should specify a primary model, a secondary model, and a rationale for each workflow

Map workflows by role (PM, engineering, data, customer success, sales, etc.)

frameworks.name: Goldilocks Prompting
frameworks.description: A framework for calibrating prompt length and specificity to give AI models the optimal amount of creative freedom — enough context to understand the goal and constraints, but enough space to apply judgment and avoid generic outputs.
when_to_apply: My AI keeps generating bland, templated outputs even though my prompt has all the details it should need
I wrote a really long system prompt but the model seems to be ignoring half of it and producing worse results than before
How do I give ChatGPT enough direction to stay on track without killing its creativity?
I need to build reusable prompt components that I can mix and match across different tasks and workflows
The AI-generated data visualizations all look the same — default bar charts, same color schemes — how do I break it out of those patterns?
principles: Prompt length is not the goal — the goal is calibrating how much freedom the model has to make its own decisions
A middle-sized prompt (~50–100 words) outperforms both very short and very long prompts roughly 80% of the time
Include just enough context for the model to understand the goal, the available tools, and the decision space
Use carefully chosen good and bad examples to give the model a sense of the dimensional space it is navigating
Warn against generic sinkholes — specific failure modes where models tend to converge toward mediocre defaults
Use pattern typing to avoid ratholing the model into overly narrow interpretations
Goldilocks prompts are designed to be stackable like Lego bricks for complex multi-domain tasks
Do not use Goldilocks prompts in multi-agent workflows or when exhaustive specification is genuinely required
steps: Identify the domain where the model is producing generic or convergent outputs
Define the goal clearly in a single sentence — what outcome do you want?
Identify the model's known default failure modes for this domain (e.g., bar charts, passive voice, symmetric grids)
Select 1–2 good examples and 1–2 bad examples that illustrate the decision boundary you care about
Write guidelines or principles that cover the right set of use cases without over-specifying every detail
Keep the total prompt to roughly 50–100 words (under 500 tokens) and test for creative headroom vs. useful constraint
Stack multiple Goldilocks prompts together for complex tasks requiring multiple domains

frameworks.name: Ten Components of Good Judgement
frameworks.description: A structured decomposition of good judgement into ten distinct, learnable capabilities that together define what it means to exercise sound decision-making in complex, high-stakes situations.
when_to_apply: I keep making decisions that seem smart at the time but blow up later — how do I figure out which part of my judgment is weak?
We're promoting someone to a role with a lot of autonomy and I need to assess whether they actually have good judgment, not just intelligence
Our team keeps solving the wrong problems — we're busy but not making progress on what matters
I want to build a leadership development program focused on practical decision-making, not just theory
A project post-mortem showed the strategy was flawed from the start — how do we prevent this kind of judgment failure next time?
principles: Find real bottlenecks instead of surface problems using a scarcity principle that shows where value migrates
Reuse patterns without overgeneralizing by pairing pattern recognition with context discrimination
Think in constraints by distinguishing what is possible versus what is possible now
Sequence bets to build momentum and create proof before resistance mounts
Practice deprioritization discipline by explicitly defending what you are NOT doing
Compound judgment through calibration via feedback loops from what worked and failed
Map the social graph by planning conviction moments instead of hoping stakeholders align
Signal accountability through ownership frameworks by stating what you will do if you are wrong
Make trade-offs visible through transparent reasoning rather than only showing polished outputs
Encode judgment into systems to shift from personal heroics to organizational capability
steps: Ask the user to describe a recent high-stakes decision they made (or are making) — what was the situation, what did they decide, and what happened?

Probe the decision against each of the ten components, asking targeted questions: (1) Bottleneck Finding — did you identify the real constraint, or did you solve a surface-level problem? (2) Pattern Recognition + Context Discrimination — did you apply a mental model from a past situation, and did you check whether this situation is actually analogous? (3) Constraint Thinking — did you distinguish what's possible in theory from what's possible given current resources, politics, and timing? (4) Bet Sequencing — did you stage your commitments to build proof and momentum, or did you go all-in upfront? (5) Deprioritization Discipline — can you explicitly defend what you chose NOT to do? (6) Calibration from Feedback — have you updated your priors based on what worked and failed in similar past decisions? (7) Social Graph Mapping — did you plan your stakeholder conviction moments, or did you hope alignment would happen organically? (8) Ownership Signaling — did you state what you would do if you were wrong? (9) Trade-off Visibility — did you show your reasoning and trade-offs transparently, or only present the polished conclusion? (10) Judgment Encoding — did you build a system or process so this kind of decision doesn't depend on you personally next time?
Identify the 2-3 components where the user's answers reveal the clearest gaps — these are the underdeveloped judgment muscles
For each weak component, give a specific, actionable recommendation the user can apply to their next decision (not generic advice — tied to their described situation)
Reframe: judgment is not a single trait but ten distinct capabilities. Advise the user on which 1-2 components to deliberately practice over the next quarter

frameworks.name: Adversarial Investigation Framework (Fighting Institutional Power Asymmetry)

principles: Investigation beats negotiation: find leverage before they know you have it by identifying categorical violations, not just expressing dissatisfaction

Most valuable work happens in the middle of the spectrum (Levels 3–4), not at the autonomous extreme
Matching the solution shape to the problem shape is the core task when working with AI

frameworks.name: AI Fluency Assessment Framework
frameworks.description: An agent-administered interview that scores a person's AI fluency across five dimensions — Prompt Mastery, Technical Understanding, Practical Application, Critical Evaluation, and Workflow Design — through targeted questions rather than self-reporting, producing a weighted composite score and prioritized improvement focus.
when_to_apply: I want to figure out where exactly my AI skills are weak so I can improve systematically instead of just experimenting randomly
We're hiring for a role that requires strong AI skills but we don't have a consistent way to evaluate candidates beyond asking 'do you use ChatGPT?'
