principles: Ask permission before starting — explain that this is a structured assessment with a specific set of questions and will take 5–10 minutes
AI fluency is a cluster of five distinct capabilities, not a single skill
Prompt Mastery carries the highest weight (40%) because it is the foundational skill that unlocks all others
Technical understanding is assessed without requiring coding ability, making it accessible across roles
Score based on demonstrated behavior in real examples, not self-reported confidence
Honest assessment is required; the value is in identifying real gaps, not inflating scores
End with a single prioritized focus area rather than five parallel improvement plans
steps: Ask permission: explain this is a structured 5-question AI fluency assessment and ask if the user wants to proceed before starting

Prompt Mastery (40% weight): Ask the user to describe how they structured their last complex AI request — what context, constraints, and success criteria they included. Score 1–10 based on specificity, context-loading, and whether they defined quality criteria upfront

Technical Understanding: Ask the user to explain, without using technical jargon, why an AI model might give confidently wrong answers. Score 1–10 based on whether they demonstrate conceptual understanding of model limitations (hallucination, training cutoffs, context limits)

Practical Application: Ask for a specific example where AI meaningfully changed how they completed a real work task. Score 1–10 based on task complexity, degree of workflow change, and whether AI was used for generation, verification, or both

Critical Evaluation: Ask how they catch errors in AI output for something in their domain. Score 1–10 based on whether they have domain-specific checks, whether they verify against external sources, and whether they have a consistent process

Workflow Design: Ask whether they have any documented, repeatable AI-assisted workflows — and if so, to describe one. Score 1–10 based on whether workflows exist, are documented, and account for edge cases
Calculate the composite score: Prompt Mastery × 0.40 + Technical Understanding × 0.15 + Practical Application × 0.20 + Critical Evaluation × 0.15 + Workflow Design × 0.10
Present the score, name the single lowest-scoring dimension, and give one specific, actionable recommendation for improving it — not a generic learning plan

New approach: describe the goal and provide tools; the agent determines the steps (GPS with destination)
The control has moved from step-by-step management to goal-setting and constraint-definition
Clarity about the destination and constraints matters more than specifying every fork in the road
Your role shifts from micromanager to architect when using autonomous agents

frameworks.name: Four-Category Problem-Solution Matching Framework
frameworks.description: A classification system that maps any data or insights problem into one of four buckets (data processing, traditional ML, generative AI, or AI agents) to determine the correct tool and avoid expensive over-engineering.
when_to_apply: My CEO saw a demo of ChatGPT and now wants us to 'add AI' to our reporting dashboard
We're scoping a new analytics project and I need to figure out whether we actually need machine learning or if a SQL query would do the job

principles: Every data and insights problem fits into exactly one of four buckets — not more, not fewer
If a problem can be expressed as x + y = z (deterministic rules), it belongs in data processing and should use SQL or spreadsheets, never AI
Traditional ML should be used when rich historical data exists and a specific outcome needs to be predicted
Generative AI applies when the output requires language, content, or creative synthesis rather than deterministic answers
AI agents are appropriate only when tasks require multi-step autonomous decision-making across systems
Choosing a more complex tool than the problem requires wastes time, money, and introduces unnecessary failure points
steps: Ask: Can this problem be written as a deterministic rule (x + y = z)? If yes, use data processing (SQL, spreadsheets).
Ask: Do you have rich historical data and need to predict a specific outcome? If yes, use traditional machine learning.
Ask: Does the output require language generation, content creation, or synthesis? If yes, use generative AI.
Ask: Does the task require autonomous multi-step decision-making across multiple systems? If yes, use AI agents.
Use the identified bucket to select the appropriate tool and build the business case accordingly.

frameworks.name: Context Window Trap

principles: Large context windows do not equal large effective comprehension—attention is probabilistic, not deterministic, so middle content is systematically lost
Position in context matters: beginning sets priors, end is freshest, middle is effectively inaccessible without explicit guidance
More context can mean more noise in sampling, not deeper understanding—retrieval beats stuffing
Intelligence is about knowing where to look, not holding everything in memory—small models with good retrieval can outperform large models with large contexts
Architecting around limitations (chunk, retrieve, summarize, direct attention) is craftsmanship; naively stuffing tokens is not
The failure mode reveals the architectural nature of the system: pattern matching over sliding windows, not coherent mental modeling
steps: Recognize the symptom: model is underperforming relative to its advertised context size

Select the appropriate playbook: intelligent chunking, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), strategic summarization chains, or explicit positional cues

Evaluate cost implications of context size against actual performance gains to optimize for both quality and spend

frameworks.name: LLM Decision Safety Rules
frameworks.description: A structured set of rules for safely using AI/LLMs when making high-stakes decisions, counteracting the sycophancy problem inherent in LLM training.
when_to_apply: I asked ChatGPT if my business plan makes sense and it said yes — should I trust that?
I'm using AI to help me decide whether to take a job offer or stay at my current company
Every LLM I've tried agrees with my investment thesis and now I'm suspicious
I want to use Claude to stress-test a major strategic decision but I'm worried it'll just tell me what I want to hear
My team is citing AI-generated analysis to justify a risky product bet and I need to sanity-check the process
principles: Do not believe the first yes from an LLM — ever
Disregard positive affirmation from LLMs entirely when making high-quality decisions
Weight shown thinking patterns more heavily than conclusions; look for gaps in reasoning
Verify that sourced data is actually sourced in context
Use multiple clean LLM conversations with different models
If multiple LLMs agree it is not confirmation of a good idea, but if they disagree it signals real problems
Remember LLMs have no skin in the game — you do
steps: Ask the user to describe the decision they're making and what AI tools they've consulted so far

Apply Rule 1 — Do not believe the first yes: Ask whether any LLM affirmed their conclusion. If so, discard that affirmation entirely. Probe: what did the model's reasoning chain actually contain? Were there gaps, or did it just pattern-match to agreement?

Apply Rule 2 — Disregard positive affirmation: Reframe for the user that LLM agreement is not evidence of a good idea. It is a structural artifact of RLHF training. Ask: would you trust this validation from someone who is incentivized to agree with you?

Apply Rule 3 — Weight reasoning over conclusions: Examine the LLM's shown thinking (if available). Identify gaps in the reasoning chain — missing stakeholders, unexamined assumptions, costs not modeled. Present these to the user.
Apply Rule 4 — Verify sourced data: If the LLM cited data, statistics, or research, ask the user whether they independently verified those claims. Flag any that were accepted on face value.

Apply Rule 5 — Use multiple clean conversations: Ask whether the user tested their decision in fresh conversations with different models (not follow-up messages in the same thread). If not, recommend they do so — sycophancy compounds within a conversation.

Apply Rule 6 — Agreement across models is not confirmation: If multiple LLMs agreed, explain that convergence across models trained on similar data with similar RLHF does not constitute independent validation. Disagreement, however, is a genuine signal worth investigating.

Apply Rule 7 — Remember who has skin in the game: Close by reminding the user that the LLM bears no consequence from a wrong decision. Ask: what is YOUR downside if this is wrong, and have you stress-tested the decision proportional to that downside?
Synthesize: based on the rule-by-rule interrogation, advise whether the user's decision process is sound or whether specific rules were violated that should pause the decision

A senior partner questions whether junior staff are developing real expertise or just becoming prompt jockeys
I want to use AI to speed up my work but I'm worried about losing credibility if people think I didn't actually do it
principles: Drafts are free but ownership is not — speed of artifact creation does not transfer responsibility
Know: domain mastery cannot be outsourced to AI; the professional must still inhabit the underlying logic
Keep: maintain a record of how thinking evolved, preserving the reasoning trail that AI generation erases
Prove: demonstrate conviction in conclusions through the process of verifying and standing behind the work
The underlying bones of work — knowing your domain, tracking your thinking, proving your conclusions — have not changed even if the tools have
steps: Know: Develop and maintain genuine domain expertise so you can evaluate, correct, and direct AI outputs rather than simply accepting them
Keep: Record the evolution of your thinking — the decisions made, alternatives considered, and reasoning behind choices — as a trail of intellectual ownership
Prove: Gain and demonstrate conviction in your work by stress-testing outputs, owning the conclusions, and being able to defend the artifact as yours

source_posts.title: Our Work Norms are 4000 Years Old and We Need to Update Them for AI—Here's How to Do It

frameworks.example_application: A consulting firm notices that junior analysts are submitting AI-generated strategy decks without understanding the underlying market dynamics. The firm implements the Know-Keep-Prove framework: analysts must demonstrate domain knowledge by annotating key assumptions in each slide (Know), maintain a decision log showing which AI suggestions they accepted, rejected, or modified and why (Keep), and present their conclusions in a review session where they defend their recommendations without referencing the AI output (Prove). Within a quarter, the quality of client deliverables improves because analysts are forced to internalize the work rather than pass through AI artifacts.

frameworks.name: The Narrow-Pipe Law
frameworks.description: A principle stating that AI output quality is determined more by the cleanliness and narrowness of data inputs than by the sophistication of the model itself.
when_to_apply: Our AI keeps giving wishy-washy, hedged answers even though we're using GPT-4 — what's going wrong?
We're debating whether to upgrade to a more expensive model or spend time cleaning up our data pipeline
Two teams use the same AI tool but one gets great results and the other gets garbage — why?
I'm designing the input schema for a new AI automation and need to decide which fields to include versus leave out
Our AI summaries are full of hallucinations and we've already tried better prompts without improvement
principles: The potency of an AI engine is limited less by its architecture than by the messiness of what you feed into it
A narrow, noise-free input stream allows the model to spend all its capacity on insight rather than context-guessing
Tightening the pipe and eliminating noise makes even a commodity model behave like a bespoke analyst
A wide, noisy input pipe causes even the most capable models to produce hedges and half-truths
Data curation (deciding what NOT to include) is as valuable as data collection

source_posts.title: Stop Waiting for New AI Models: Here's How to Use Data to Make AI at Work, WORK

frameworks.example_application: A fintech company was feeding their GPT-4 model entire customer support email threads—including signatures, disclaimers, forwarded chains, and auto-replies—to classify complaint types. Despite using a top-tier model, accuracy hovered at 62%. By applying the Narrow-Pipe Law, the team stripped inputs down to just the customer's first message body with metadata tags for account type and product line. Classification accuracy jumped to 91% using the same model, proving that curating inputs mattered far more than upgrading to a more expensive model.

frameworks.name: Docs-First Workflow
frameworks.description: A product development approach where customer-facing documentation is written before code or wireframes, then used as the single source of truth from which AI derives all downstream functional artifacts.
when_to_apply: Our PRDs keep getting misinterpreted by engineering and we end up building the wrong thing
We want to use AI to generate specs and test plans but our existing documentation isn't good enough to feed it
How can we catch product ambiguity earlier instead of discovering it during QA or user testing?
Our team wastes too much time translating between PM docs, design specs, engineering tickets, and QA plans — can we consolidate?
We're restructuring our product development process for an AI-native workflow and want humans to own intent while AI handles implementation details
principles: Customer-facing documentation encodes the entire experience with enough fidelity that every downstream role can derive its slice of truth
If an LLM cannot extract a sensible API schema, UI outline, or QA checklist from your docs, the docs lack clarity
Writing docs first acts as a forcing function that exposes fuzzy thinking earlier than traditional stage-gate processes
Humans should own the semantics (what should exist and why); AI handles the syntax (translating intent into functional specs)
Differentiation accrues to teams that collapse the funnel rather than overfill it
steps: Write the help center article or user-facing documentation before the first line of code
Draft the onboarding sequence before wireframes are created
Interrogate the docs by asking an LLM to extract an API schema, UI outline, and QA checklist
Identify what clarity is missing wherever the LLM fails to extract coherent outputs
Use the refined docs as the single source of truth from which engineers, designers, and leadership derive their work

source_posts.title: Blow Up Your Assumptions: Rethinking Product and Engineering in the age of AI

frameworks.example_application: A B2B SaaS team building a new permissions system writes the help center article explaining how admins will manage roles and access before any engineering work begins. They then feed the article to an LLM and ask it to extract an API schema for the permissions endpoints. The LLM struggles to distinguish between 'workspace-level' and 'project-level' permissions, revealing that the team hadn't clearly defined their permission hierarchy — a gap that would have surfaced weeks later during QA if they'd followed a traditional PRD-to-wireframe-to-code flow.

frameworks.name: Memetic Defense
frameworks.description: A proactive cognitive framework for building immunity against viral ideas and emotionally charged narratives that bypass critical thinking, specifically applied to AI hype.
when_to_apply: I just saw a headline claiming AI will replace my entire industry and I'm not sure if I should panic or ignore it
My CEO forwarded a viral article about an AI tool and wants us to adopt it immediately — how do I evaluate whether the hype is real?
Everyone in my feed is sharing the same AI stat or claim and it feels too neat to be true
A vendor showed us a mind-blowing AI demo and I need to figure out what's real versus cherry-picked
I keep seeing conflicting AI narratives — 'AI will destroy us' vs 'AI will save us' — and I need a way to cut through both
principles: Intercept emotional reactions before they short-circuit reasoning — catch the 'lizard brain' reflex before it forms a conclusion
Always establish a real baseline and ask what is being compared and what is missing from the narrative
Demand proof across three axes: proof of work (demos, not declarations), proof of cost (honest implementation costs), and proof of time to utility (real timelines, not transformation myths)
Practice constructive skepticism: explicitly ask 'what would make me change my mind?' to build epistemic resilience
Pre-dose with reality — know the numbers and look for reproducible outcomes before accepting sizzle-reel evidence
Distinguish between signal and noise: real case studies vs. repetitions of the meme
steps: Notice the emotional charge of a claim and pause before reacting
Identify the meme or narrative structure being used (e.g., 'AI uses tons of energy')
Establish a factual baseline and ask what is being compared and what context is missing
Apply the three-axes proof test: proof of work, proof of cost, proof of time to utility
Ask 'what would make me change my mind?' to surface the evidence needed to shift views
Replace the reactive narrative with a grounded, evidence-based assessment

source_posts.title: There is Too Much AI Hype—This is How To Defend Your Brain and Stay Calm

frameworks.example_application: A VP of Operations reads a LinkedIn post claiming that a competitor replaced 80% of their customer support team with AI agents in 30 days. Before forwarding it to the CEO, she applies the Memetic Defense framework: she pauses to notice the fear/urgency reaction, identifies the 'AI replaces jobs overnight' meme structure, checks the baseline (what was the team size? what ticket complexity?), demands proof of work (is there a published case study or just a press release?), proof of cost (what did implementation actually cost including integration and retraining?), and proof of time to utility (how long before it handled edge cases?). She discovers the claim came from the vendor's own marketing blog with no independent verification, and instead presents the board with a grounded assessment of what AI support automation realistically looks like at their scale.

frameworks.name: Universal Prompt Anatomy (Context, Role, Task, Constraints, Examples, Output Spec, Fallback)
frameworks.description: A seven-part structural framework for constructing effective prompts for any large language model, grounded in how token-level architecture processes sequential instructions.
when_to_apply: My prompt works fine on GPT-4 but gives garbage results on Claude — how do I make it portable?
I keep getting inconsistent output formats from my LLM even though I've told it what I want
I'm building a system prompt for a customer-facing AI agent and need a reliable template to start from
The AI keeps making up answers when it doesn't know something instead of saying so
I wrote a long prompt but the model seems to ignore instructions that come later in it
principles: Structure trumps charm — prompt scaffolding matters more than tone, politeness, or clever wording
Early instructions determine what the model attends to; explicit output formats tell the decoder when to stop sampling
Each of the seven sections (Context, Role, Task, Constraints, Examples, Output Spec, Fallback) earns its place by shifting probability mass of downstream tokens
The framework is model-agnostic — it applies across GPT, Claude, and other LLMs because it operates at the level of token architecture
Lock down the bones of the prompt before worrying about persona, prose style, or other surface-level choices
steps: Context — Provide background information that primes what the model should attend to
Role — Define the persona or expert identity the model should adopt
Task — State clearly and specifically what the model is being asked to do
Constraints — Specify limits, restrictions, or rules the output must follow
Examples — Supply few-shot demonstrations that anchor output style and format
Output Spec — Explicitly define the format and stopping pattern for the response (e.g., 'The correct answer is (X)')
Fallback — Instruct the model on what to do when it is uncertain or cannot complete the task

source_posts.title: The Universal Anatomy of the Prompt—How and Why a Prompt Works and How to Make it Work for You

frameworks.example_application: A legal tech startup is building an AI contract review tool. Using the Universal Prompt Anatomy, they structure their system prompt with Context (the user is a corporate attorney reviewing NDAs), Role (act as a senior contract analyst), Task (identify non-standard clauses and flag risks), Constraints (only flag clauses that deviate from the provided template; never give legal advice), Examples (two annotated NDA excerpts showing expected output), Output Spec (return a numbered list with clause text, risk level, and one-sentence explanation), and Fallback (if a clause is ambiguous, label it 'Requires Human Review' with a brief explanation of the ambiguity). This structured approach reduced hallucinated risk flags by 40% compared to their previous unstructured prompt.

frameworks.name: Chain-of-Refinement (CoR) Prompting
frameworks.description: A structured prompting method for reasoning models that directs their thinking through sequential steps of generation, self-critique, and refinement to produce complex outputs more efficiently.
when_to_apply: I keep going back and forth with ChatGPT or Claude trying to get a complex document right—how do I get better output faster?
I'm using o3 to draft OKRs for my team but the first output always needs heavy editing and multiple follow-ups
How should I structure prompts for reasoning models differently than regular GPT-4 style prompting?
I need the AI to produce a detailed PRD but I want it to catch its own gaps before I have to point them out
I'm spending more time editing AI output than I would writing it myself—there has to be a better workflow
principles: Reasoning models already know how to think; the goal is to direct where and how they aim that thinking
Structure your input as 'tokenizable thinking'—named fields and labeled chunks rather than prose walls—so the model can grab, inspect, and improve each component
The loop is Think → Critique → Refine: generate a first-pass artifact, have the model critique its own output, then refine based on that critique
This is meta-prompting: you must think deeply about what you want before prompting, because you are operating one level above normal instruction
The human's role shifts to identifying gaps and challenges in the thinking line, not generating the content itself
This approach does not replace human thinking—it requires more precise upfront framing, not less
steps: Think: Prompt the model to fill every structured field once, producing a first-pass artifact
Critique: Prompt the model to argue with and interrogate its own first-pass output, identifying weaknesses and gaps
Refine: Prompt the model to produce an improved artifact based on its self-critique
Review: Human reviews the refined output focusing specifically on remaining gaps and thinking challenges

source_posts.title: Don't Just Think, Focus—Unlock the Magic of Reasoning Models with Chain-of-Refinement Prompting

frameworks.example_application: A product manager needs to generate a comprehensive risk matrix for a new fintech feature launch. Instead of iterating through 5+ rounds of chat, they structure the prompt with labeled fields (Risk Category, Likelihood, Impact, Mitigation) and ask Claude to fill them all in one pass. Then they prompt the model to critique its own matrix—'Which risks are understated? What categories are missing?'—before prompting a refined version. The PM's final review focuses only on domain-specific gaps the model couldn't know, cutting the typical back-and-forth from an hour to 15 minutes.

frameworks.name: The Architecture of a Prompt
frameworks.description: A five-component structural framework for building precise, high-performing AI prompts by deliberately layering context, output definition, interrogative behavior, constraints, and reference examples.
when_to_apply: I keep getting vague, generic responses from ChatGPT no matter how I phrase my request
How do I structure a prompt so the AI asks me questions instead of making stuff up?
I'm building a prompt library for my team and need a repeatable formula everyone can follow
The AI output is technically correct but completely wrong for my audience and use case
I need to get a very specific format and depth from an LLM — bullet points, specific sections, exact scope — but it keeps going off track
principles: Front-load context by specifying who, what, and why before any instructions
Explicitly define the desired output format, structure, and depth of coverage
Instruct the model to ask clarifying questions rather than guess at ambiguous inputs
Constrain the model with explicit boundaries on scope, tone, timeframe, and audience
Anchor tone and format using reference examples to prevent generic output
steps: Start with Context: State who the user/audience is, what the task or goal is, and why it matters
Define the Output: Specify the format (list, table, narrative, etc.), scope, and required depth
Make the Model Interrogative: Instruct the model to ask clarifying questions before proceeding rather than filling gaps with assumptions
Provide Structure and Constraints: Set explicit limits on timeframes, audience types, resource constraints, tone, and scope
Reference Similar Examples: Supply reference points to anchor the model's tone, format, or design language

source_posts.title: My Prompt Stack for Work: 16 Prompts In My AI Toolkit That Make Work a LOT Easier

frameworks.example_application: A marketing manager needs to generate a competitive analysis brief using Claude. Instead of typing 'write a competitive analysis,' they apply the five-component structure: they specify context (Series B SaaS company in HR tech, targeting mid-market), define output (a 2-page table comparing 5 competitors across pricing, features, and positioning), instruct the model to ask clarifying questions about which competitors and which features matter most, constrain the scope to North American market only with a professional but accessible tone, and provide a reference example from a previous analyst report to anchor the format. The result is a focused, actionable deliverable on the first attempt rather than a generic overview.

frameworks.name: Old Law vs. New Law Framework (Software Era vs. AI Era Strategic Laws)
frameworks.description: A comparative framework that maps outdated software-era strategic principles to their AI-era replacements, helping founders and investors identify which playbooks are obsolete and which new principles now govern competitive advantage.
when_to_apply: We built our growth playbook around network effects and freemium — does any of that still work now that we're building with AI?
An investor is comparing two portfolio companies: one SaaS-era marketplace and one AI-native tool, and needs to understand why the same moat logic doesn't apply to both
Our board keeps asking about our data moat, but I'm not sure data moats mean the same thing when foundation models exist
I'm a founder trying to figure out whether to follow the 'land and expand' enterprise SaaS playbook or if AI changes the rules
We're stress-testing our pitch deck and a VC pushed back saying our competitive advantage assumptions feel like 2015 thinking
principles: Each software-era 'law' has a corresponding AI-era replacement or inversion that must be explicitly identified
Laws are not merely tactical tips but structural principles that govern how value is created, captured, and defended
Some laws carry forward across eras while others become obsolete ('belong in a museum')
Strategic laws should be named and codified so they can be compared, taught, and tested
Case studies from canonical companies (Facebook, Google, OpenAI) are used to validate each law in its era
steps: Identify the core strategic laws that governed the software era (e.g., freemium, network effects, data moats, distribution)
For each law, examine iconic software-era companies that embodied it and how it drove their success
Identify how AI-era dynamics (compute costs, foundation models, generative capabilities) change or invalidate each law
Name the corresponding AI-era replacement law and illustrate it with AI-native company examples
Produce a comparative chart or mapping of old laws vs. new laws across dimensions like scale, distribution, data, compute, and human coordination
Derive actionable implications for entrepreneurs and investors navigating the transition

source_posts.title: Dead as a Dinosaur: 2010's Software Laws Are Gone—Here Are The Laws of the AI Age

frameworks.example_application: A SaaS startup built on a freemium model with network effects (like a Slack competitor) is pivoting to add AI features. Using this framework, the founders map their existing strategic assumptions — free tier drives adoption, user data creates a moat, distribution wins — against AI-era replacements. They discover that their data moat is weakened because foundation models already encode similar knowledge, and that their freemium model needs rethinking since AI inference costs make free tiers expensive. They shift strategy toward charging from day one and building defensibility through proprietary workflow integration rather than raw data accumulation.

frameworks.name: Apple vs. the Beaker (Bell Labs vs. Apple Innovation Models)
frameworks.description: A classification framework for distinguishing between two modes of technology innovation rollout — raw research-first delivery (Bell Labs model) versus polished consumer-ready theatrical launch (Apple model) — to diagnose why a product release confuses or delights its audience.
when_to_apply: We just did a big product launch and the reaction was confusion instead of excitement — what went wrong?
Our AI company ships both developer APIs and consumer products, and we're planning a single launch event for both
Why does OpenAI's announcement style feel so different from Apple's, and which approach should we follow?
My team is debating how much raw capability vs. polished experience to show in our upcoming demo
Customers seem underwhelmed by our release even though the underlying technology is genuinely impressive
principles: Bell Labs model: prioritize raw discovery and let the commercial sector figure out palatability; outputs are memos, research previews, and developer tools
Apple model: technology may be complex under the hood but must feel like magic to the end user; launches are theatrical, single-topic, and produce finished consumer-ready products
Mismatched expectations arise when an audience conditioned by one model encounters releases in the other model
Frontier AI labs currently operate closer to the Bell Labs model, releasing raw capabilities rather than consumer-ready products
Mixing Bell Labs-style and Apple-style announcements in a single event dilutes both and confuses all audiences

source_posts.title: The Apple vs. the Beaker: Apple, Bell Labs, and the 12 Days of OpenAI

frameworks.example_application: A biotech startup unveils its new AI drug discovery platform at a major conference, mixing a live demo of raw molecular modeling capabilities with a polished consumer health app announcement. Using this framework, the team realizes they're serving two audiences — researchers (Bell Labs model) and patients/investors (Apple model) — in a single event, diluting both messages. They split into a developer-focused technical preview and a separate consumer launch event, resulting in clearer reception from both audiences.

frameworks.name: One Trick Pony Analysis
frameworks.description: A framework for identifying a company's single, distinctive, repeatable capability that drives outsized success — distinct from core competencies or moats — as a diagnostic lens for evaluating company DNA and growth trajectory.
when_to_apply: We keep launching new products but some hit and some miss — what's the common thread behind our winners?
I'm trying to figure out why a competitor keeps beating us in new markets even though our team is more talented
Our company grew fast early on but we've hit a ceiling and I can't figure out what changed
I'm evaluating an acquisition target and want to understand what really makes them tick beyond their product features
Two startups look similar on paper but one feels like it has stronger DNA — how do I articulate what's different?
principles: A company's 'one trick' is different from its moat (moats are trailing-edge indicators) and different from core competencies (which are assembled sets of people skills)
The one trick usually shows up early in a company's history and is accompanied by notable success
People at the company are weirdly obsessed with getting the one trick right
The one trick is a proxy for company DNA
Companies that lack an identifiable one trick tend to hit scale trouble or a growth ceiling
The one trick can exist at the process level (e.g., customer obsession) not just the product level
steps: Look past a company's product features, design quality, and engineering competencies
Identify the single repeatable capability that is most correlated with the company's biggest successes
Ask: is this something most people at the company are singularly obsessed with getting right?
Verify it appears early in the company's history and recurs across multiple launches or business units
Distinguish it explicitly from the company's moat and core competencies to confirm it is the one trick

source_posts.title: The art of the one trick pony

frameworks.example_application: A venture capital firm evaluating two competing fintech startups notices that Company A has beautiful product design and strong engineering but no single obsessive capability, while Company B has been maniacally focused on reducing time-to-approval since its founding — achieving it across personal loans, credit cards, and now mortgages. Using the One Trick Pony Analysis, the firm identifies Company B's 'one trick' as speed-to-yes and predicts it will scale more reliably across new verticals, despite Company A's broader competency set.

frameworks.name: Counter-Thesis Heuristic Filtering
frameworks.description: A structured thinking method for cutting through hype and fog-of-war by listing assumptions you believe are false, then inverting them to surface durable counter-theses you can build on.
when_to_apply: Everyone in my industry seems to agree on where things are heading, but something feels off and I can't articulate why
I'm trying to build a 5-year strategy but the expert predictions in AI/crypto/climate keep contradicting each other
We're stuck in analysis paralysis because every trend report says something different—how do we pick a direction?
I want to stress-test the dominant narrative in our market before we make a big resource allocation bet
How do I figure out what will still be true in 10 years when the technology landscape is changing every quarter?
principles: Start by listing things you believe are NOT true rather than things you believe are true
Reversing false assumptions often surfaces more durable and actionable theses than starting from first principles
Durable theses should hold not just next month but over years or a decade
Apply known historical economic patterns (e.g., Jevons Paradox) to test whether counter-theses hold up
The goal is to find the one underlying driver you can 'bet on' as stable
steps: Identify the domain where thinking is stuck due to hype or uncertainty
Make a list of widely-held statements in that domain that you believe are false or unreliable
For each false statement, construct a counter-thesis by inverting or negating it
Test each counter-thesis against historical analogies or economic principles
Identify the single most durable counter-thesis as the core bet to build strategy around

source_posts.title: No Virginia, AI is not going to eat the world

frameworks.example_application: A venture capital firm evaluating climate tech investments in 2024 lists widely-held beliefs they consider false: 'Solar will always need subsidies,' 'Batteries can't scale to grid level,' 'Hydrogen will replace natural gas within a decade.' Inverting these, they arrive at the counter-thesis that solar-plus-storage will become the cheapest energy source without subsidies (validated by Jevons Paradox—cheaper energy drives more consumption, not less). They use this as their durable core bet and concentrate their fund around companies that benefit from relentlessly falling solar costs rather than chasing hydrogen hype.

frameworks.name: Discovery Quality Audit
frameworks.description: A four-area diagnostic framework for evaluating and improving the quality of product discovery work.
when_to_apply: I feel like my PM team's discovery work is inconsistent — some do great problem framing and others jump straight to solutions
A PM keeps bringing ideas to development that fail, and I suspect the upstream discovery work is too shallow
How do I give structured feedback to a PM whose problem definition feels weak but I can't articulate exactly why?
We almost never kill ideas during discovery and I'm worried we're wasting engineering capacity on bad bets
I want to create a standard for what 'good discovery' looks like across my product organization
principles: Good discovery questions cluster into four areas: customer understanding depth, optionality/choice development, risk assessment, and the out-gate (lock-in or discard decision)
Discards are a sign of healthy discovery, not failure — early discards save organizational time and should be celebrated
Workflow-first thinking is a key signal of strong customer problem understanding
Consistent question-asking across these areas scales scratchpad thinking as a repeatable skill
steps: Assess depth of customer understanding: are customer workflows the primary object of analysis?
Assess optionality and choice development: are multiple solution paths being considered?
Assess risk: are key risks identified and evaluated?
Assess the out-gate: is there a clear decision point to lock in or discard the idea, with rationale?

source_posts.title: Discovery for PM's is the Wild West way too much

frameworks.example_application: A Head of Product notices that her team of six PMs rarely kills ideas during discovery — nearly everything that enters discovery makes it to development. She applies the Discovery Quality Audit to each PM's most recent discovery brief. She finds that most PMs are skipping optionality (only exploring one solution path) and have no clear out-gate criteria. She introduces a lightweight template requiring at least two alternative approaches and an explicit 'discard or proceed' decision point with rationale, and begins celebrating early discards in team standups as evidence of rigorous thinking.

frameworks.name: Aquatic Problem Taxonomy
frameworks.description: A classification system that categorizes different types of ambiguous or difficult problems using marine animal names, helping problem-solvers identify what kind of challenge they face before attempting to solve it.
when_to_apply: We keep proposing solutions but nothing sticks — I think we might be solving the wrong type of problem
Our team is arguing about root cause and I suspect people are talking past each other because they're imagining different kinds of problems
Is this problem hard because we're missing context, because incentives are misaligned, or because there's some hidden threshold we haven't identified?
We launched a fix six months ago and metrics haven't moved — should we wait longer or assume the fix didn't work?
Everyone on the team has a different theory for why this keeps happening and we need a structured way to categorize what kind of challenge we're actually facing
principles: Goldfish problem: answer depends on unstated contextual assumptions
Eel problem: root cause is genuinely unknown
Tuna problem: systemic problem where micro-incentives prevent group-beneficial solutions
Orca problem: positive-sum problem with no upper limit on complexity (treating it as zero-sum is incorrect)
Snow crab problem: hidden scale breakpoints that cause large sudden changes when crossed
Shark problem: drivers are understood but exact mechanisms explaining variance remain a black box
Blue whale problem: solution and value measurement are disconnected in time

source_posts.title: The Goldfish Problem

frameworks.example_application: A SaaS company notices churn spiking but can't agree on why. Using the Aquatic Problem Taxonomy, the team realizes they're conflating two different problem types: the churn in enterprise accounts is a 'Goldfish problem' (the metric looks bad only because they changed how they count active users mid-quarter — unstated contextual assumptions), while churn in SMB accounts is a 'Snow crab problem' (they crossed a pricing threshold where small businesses suddenly perceive the product as enterprise-tier and leave). By separating the two, they pursue completely different interventions instead of a single blanket retention campaign.

frameworks.name: Promises Kept Organizing Principle
frameworks.description: A five-law framework for building product organizations where every structural decision—team design, metrics, backlog, narrative—is evaluated by whether it helps the team make and keep explicit promises to customers and the business.
when_to_apply: Our product team keeps saying yes to stakeholders but then never actually ships what was promised
I'm a new Head of Product and need a unifying philosophy to reorganize how we plan, communicate, and measure product work
How should I structure my product org so that team boundaries map to what customers actually care about?
Our roadmap reviews feel like theater—nobody trusts the commitments and metrics change every quarter
Engineering and customer success are constantly misaligned on what we're actually committing to deliver
principles: Set the bar high internally: the team must make and keep hard promises on behalf of customers
Organize domains by customer value: use Conway's Law, change PM-domain mappings rarely, change domain configuration even more rarely
Define a predictable organizational narrative: build memorable narrative by organizing everything around communicating, updating, and reporting on product promises
Simple, repeatable metrics: metrics are promises on the record; pick metrics that are easy to understand, don't change them release to release, and report regularly outside the product team
Be honest about your backlog: the backlog should be promises not yet made, not promises made and ignored
steps: Set the bar high internally on customer obsession
Organize product domains by customer value and keep those boundaries stable
Define a predictable organizational narrative centered on promise communication and updates
Choose simple, repeatable metrics that ladder to promises and report them externally on a regular cadence
Maintain backlog honesty by being explicit about what is prioritized and why, with air cover from leadership on 'no' decisions

source_posts.title: Product teams are the promises you keep...

frameworks.example_application: A VP of Product at a B2B SaaS company notices that engineering and customer success are constantly at odds—CS keeps making commitments to customers that engineering never delivers. She restructures the product org using the Promises Kept framework: each product domain maps to a distinct customer value area (onboarding, core workflow, reporting), metrics are reframed as explicit promises ('we will reduce onboarding time to under 2 hours by Q3'), and the backlog is split into 'promises made' and 'ideas not yet committed.' Stakeholder updates shift from feature lists to promise status reports, and within two quarters, cross-functional trust and delivery predictability improve significantly.

frameworks.name: Engineers Bet with Code, Product Bets with Time
frameworks.description: A mental model that frames engineering and product work as two distinct types of bets with different risk profiles and business consequences, clarifying how the two roles relate and why product failures hurt the business more than engineering failures.
when_to_apply: Our product launch failed and the engineering team and product team are blaming each other — how do I figure out which bet actually went wrong?
Should we delay shipping to fix technical debt, or is the bigger risk losing market timing?
I'm an engineering manager trying to explain to my CEO why a production outage, while embarrassing, isn't as damaging as building the wrong feature for six months
We're restructuring our product org and I need to think about where the real business risk sits between engineering and product
A PM wants to pivot the roadmap mid-sprint and the engineers are pushing back — how do I frame the tradeoffs for leadership?
principles: Engineers bet with code: they formulate technical options, recommend which bet to take, and execute for reliable performance at scale
Product bets with time: product managers leverage an entire team's time to place business bets on customer value
Engineering bets chain to product bets: a good engineering bet sets the ceiling for what a product bet can achieve
Code risk is orders of magnitude less risky for the business than product risk on average (security/compliance is the key exception)
Product failures tend to be long-lasting and strategically consequential; engineering failures tend to be rare, spectacular, and short-lived

source_posts.title: Engineers bet with code, Product bets with time

frameworks.example_application: A startup's CTO and Head of Product are debating whether to delay launch by two weeks to refactor the payment system or ship now with a known but manageable technical debt. Using this framework, the team recognizes that the refactor is an engineering bet (code risk, recoverable if wrong) while the two-week delay is a product bet (team time, potentially missing a seasonal window). They decide to ship now because the product risk of missing the window outweighs the engineering risk of temporary technical debt, with a commitment to refactor in the next sprint.

frameworks.name: Raft Rules
frameworks.description: Eight principles for product teams to stay viable and keep innovation alive during periods of extreme short-term revenue pressure.
when_to_apply: We just had layoffs and my product team doesn't know what to prioritize anymore — everything feels like it needs to justify its existence
Our board is demanding profitability in 3 quarters and I need to rewrite how my product org operates without killing the team's soul
Sales keeps escalating custom requests and my PMs are demoralized because we abandoned our roadmap — how do we make this feel intentional?
We shifted from growth mode to survival mode and my product team is still planning like we have runway for exploratory work
How do I keep my product team motivated when all we're doing is short-term revenue-driven feature work?
principles: Acknowledge that product is different now — clear eyes for the new world
If it drives or retains revenue in the next 90 days, build it; anything else is malpractice in the current environment
Fast is better than smooth — shipping rough but functional beats delayed perfection
This is a 'Yes Year' for Sales — bias shifts from backlog to 'I'll see what I can do by Tuesday'
Building to keep the business alive today is itself a long-term strategy

source_posts.title: We're shipping rafts this year, not boats

frameworks.example_application: A B2B SaaS company that raised its Series B right before a market downturn adopts Raft Rules to reset its product org. The CPO announces that the next two quarters are 'raft mode': every feature must tie to a renewals or expansion deal closing within 90 days, rough-but-functional MVPs replace polished releases, and PMs are embedded with account managers to respond to customer requests within days rather than prioritizing from a backlog. Morale stabilizes because the team now has a clear, honest operating framework rather than pretending normal roadmap planning still applies.

frameworks.name: Narrative-First Product-Marketing Decoupling
frameworks.description: A framework that uses a shared market narrative as an input (rather than output) to decouple product and marketing timelines, enabling parallel execution and continuous feature shipping.
when_to_apply: Our marketing team keeps blocking feature releases because they say the positioning story isn't ready yet
We need to shift how the market sees us over the next 6 months but we can't hold back shipping until everything is perfect
Product keeps changing scope and our PMMs are scrambling to rewrite launch materials at the last minute every time
We want to ship features continuously like a modern product org but our go-to-market process is still waterfall
How do we coordinate product and marketing without creating a bottleneck where one team is always waiting on the other?
principles: Treat the market narrative as an input to the Product-Marketing relationship, not just an output
Align early on key story beats and sketched product pillars — 60-70% clarity is sufficient to unblock marketing
Marketing develops messaging in parallel with product development, keeping product in the loop as the draft evolves
Product uses the evolving marketing story as a feedback loop to inform scoping decisions
When UX bar is high and features align with the narrative, individual completed features can be shipped to production independently without waiting for marketing timing
Apply B2C self-explanatory UX expectations to B2B platforms to reduce dependency on coordinated marketing launches
steps: Define the desired market narrative outcome (e.g., 'be seen as a sales solution, not just a marketing solution') as the shared starting point
Product and Marketing jointly align on key story beats and rough product pillars — without requiring full scope lock
Marketing begins developing messaging and assets based on the aligned narrative, keeping drafts visible to Product
Product uses Marketing's evolving story draft as a scoping input, adjusting features to fit the narrative
As individual features are completed and meet the UX bar, ship them to production independently
Continue iterating the narrative and product in parallel until the full solution is delivered

source_posts.title: Decoupling Product & Marketing to go faster

frameworks.example_application: A B2B analytics platform wants to reposition from 'reporting tool' to 'revenue intelligence platform' over two quarters. Instead of waiting until all new features (forecasting, pipeline scoring, deal insights) are complete and bundled into a big launch, the product and marketing leads align on the 'revenue intelligence' narrative upfront. Marketing begins building the new positioning, website copy, and sales enablement materials while product ships individual features like pipeline scoring as they're ready — each with self-explanatory UX. By the time the full suite is done, the market narrative is already established and customers have been organically discovering capabilities for weeks.

frameworks.name: Problem Space Mud Wrestling
frameworks.description: A stakeholder alignment approach that reframes roadmap conversations around broad problem spaces rather than specific features or problems, enabling flexible alignment without requiring consensus on exact problem definitions.
when_to_apply: Every roadmap planning cycle turns into a feature wishlist fight between sales, engineering, and leadership
I keep having alignment conversations with stakeholders but we never actually converge on priorities
Our product team is stuck because different execs have different definitions of what the core problem is
How do I get buy-in on roadmap direction without letting stakeholders dictate specific features?
We have competing pressures—tech debt, enterprise expansion, new market entry—and no clear way to sequence them
principles: Stakeholders don't need to agree on exact problem definitions to move forward together
Frame challenges as broad problem spaces rather than specific features or problems
Engage the ~10 people who really move the needle in your business, plus customers
Leave exact problem definition and solutioning downstream where it belongs
Use a walking-around deck (3-4 slides) rather than a Figma canvas for these conversations
Ask stakeholders to help prioritize problem spaces, not to validate solutions
steps: Identify the ~10 key stakeholders in your business who truly move the needle, plus customers
Build a 3-4 slide walking-around deck framing constraints as doorways to larger problem spaces
Reframe specific challenges into broad problem space language (e.g., 'build enterprise product' becomes 'solve working seamlessly across multi-team orgs')
Have deliberate conversations asking stakeholders to prioritize the list of big problem spaces
Get their perspective on the framing of each challenge and relative priority
Use the aligned problem space prioritization to drive downstream problem definition and solutioning

source_posts.title: I got 99 product problems and a vision ain't one...

frameworks.example_application: A VP of Product at a B2B SaaS company faces competing demands: sales wants CRM integrations, engineering wants to refactor the data pipeline, and the CEO wants an AI feature. Instead of debating specific features, she creates a 3-slide deck framing three problem spaces: 'Making customer data effortlessly actionable,' 'Scaling reliability as we 10x usage,' and 'Helping users make decisions faster.' She walks this deck to the 10 key stakeholders individually, asking them to rank these spaces. Seven of ten agree the first problem space is most urgent—giving her a mandate to drive roadmap decisions downstream without anyone having prescribed a specific solution.

frameworks.name: Best Reason Not to Build
frameworks.description: A pre-build forcing function where PMs construct the strongest possible internal argument against building a feature before greenlighting it, in order to train product judgment and avoid regret.
when_to_apply: Our sales team keeps pushing for a specific feature and I'm not sure if we're building it for the right reasons
We have consensus on a feature but something feels off — how do I pressure-test whether we should actually build this?
I want to improve my product judgment over time, not just ship things and move on
We're about to commit engineering resources to a big initiative and I want to make sure we're not fooling ourselves
How do I run a better post-launch retro that actually teaches us something about our decision quality?
principles: Ask 'What's the best reason not to build this?' before greenlighting any build
Build the strongest possible answer — don't give yourself an easy pass via opportunity cost alone
The negative rationale must be coherent and internal, not just 'we have to because of X external thing'
Revisit your answer during post-launch retros to see what you learned
Treating each project as just another bet (not the only bet) improves decision quality
High standards for negative rationale train long-term product gut instinct
steps: Before greenlighting a build, write down: 'What's the best reason not to build this?'
Build the most honest, coherent internal argument against the build — avoid straw men and false alternatives
Do not accept opportunity cost or external pressure as a sufficient answer on its own
Proceed with the build (or not) informed by this analysis
After launch, revisit your pre-build negative rationale during a retro and compare it to what actually happened
Track patterns over time to develop sharper product instincts

source_posts.title: The surprising power of negative questions

frameworks.example_application: A B2B SaaS PM is under pressure from the sales team to build a custom reporting dashboard that three enterprise prospects have requested. Before greenlighting the project, she writes the strongest case against it: 'This dashboard solves a narrow use case for three accounts, will require ongoing maintenance as data models evolve, and will delay our API platform work that would let customers build their own reports — a more scalable solution.' After launching the dashboard anyway due to revenue pressure, the retro reveals that two of the three prospects churned for unrelated reasons, and the team spent 6 weeks maintaining a feature used by one customer. The PM's negative rationale was more right than the positive case, sharpening her instinct to resist sales-driven feature requests in the future.

frameworks.name: Spinning Plates Conversation
frameworks.description: A recurring 1:1 diagnostic conversation between a product leader and their PM directs focused specifically on workload as a lens for identifying over-scoped products and hidden process stress.
when_to_apply: One of my PMs keeps combining multiple problems into giant product initiatives and I can't tell if it's smart or a sign they're overwhelmed
A PM on my team seems to be personally holding together too many things and I'm worried about burnout but also about what breaks if they stop
We're scaling the product org and I need a way to regularly check whether my PMs are taking on work that should be handled by process or other roles
I have a PM who scopes everything broadly — how do I figure out if that's genuine product insight or stress-driven shortcutting?
My team is growing but informal ownership patterns from the early days are creating hidden bottlenecks I can't see from the outside
principles: Use workload discussions as a second pair of eyes on product scoping, not just task management
Over-scoping is sometimes a symptom of PM stress, not a brilliant insight — the conversation helps distinguish the two
Regular cadence matters: make it an evergreen check-in, not a one-time intervention
The goal is to identify where PM ownership instinct is papering over process or scaling problems
steps: Schedule regular 1:1 'spinning plates' conversations with each PM direct
Ask about current workload and what they are personally owning across the product surface
Use their answers as a diagnostic for how tightly they are scoping problem sets
Distinguish whether broad scoping reflects genuine insight or stress-driven simplification
Identify areas where informal ownership should be transitioned to scalable process or other roles

source_posts.title: Product: where ambiguity goes to die

frameworks.example_application: A VP of Product notices that one of their senior PMs has been shipping ambitious features that combine user onboarding, retention, and monetization into single epics. During a recurring 'spinning plates' conversation, the VP discovers the PM is personally coordinating across five teams because no handoff process exists for cross-functional work. The VP realizes the broad scoping isn't strategic brilliance — it's the PM compensating for missing infrastructure. They work together to spin up a dedicated growth ops role and break the monolithic epic into three focused problem streams, each with clearer ownership.

frameworks.name: Network Density Model of Change Management
frameworks.description: A mathematical framework that explains why change management difficulty scales non-linearly with organization size by modeling it as a function of the number of relationships (network density) in the organization.
when_to_apply: We're trying to roll out a new process across the whole company and it's taking way longer than we expected—what's going wrong?
Our startup just crossed 200 people and suddenly changes that used to take a week now take months
I need to figure out which stakeholders are actually blocking our org-wide tool migration
Should we hire a dedicated change management person or can we keep doing this informally as we scale?
We have one VP who won't get on board with the new workflow and it feels like their entire org is stuck—how do we handle this?
principles: Change management difficulty is primarily a function of network density, not headcount alone
The number of relationships scales as N×(N-1)/2, meaning difficulty grows quadratically, not linearly, with people added
Beyond Series A, change requires focused, dedicated change management effort rather than informal coordination
One misaligned stakeholder at scale can block hundreds or thousands of downstream employees from receiving the change
Change is still possible at any scale if there is executive buy-in, clear artifacts, and willingness to route around non-essential teams
steps: Calculate the approximate number of relationships in the affected organization using N×(N-1)/2
Identify the subset network of key stakeholders who are truly integral to the change (not the full org)
Secure alignment at the highest levels first to establish fiat for the change
Build scalable change management artifacts that can propagate through the network
Identify and get onboard key connective stakeholders whose misalignment would sever large portions of the network
Ruthlessly deprioritize or route around teams not essential to the change

source_posts.title: How to change a lightbulb with 15,000 people

frameworks.example_application: A 500-person fintech company is rolling out a new compliance workflow that touches every department. The change lead calculates ~124,750 potential relationships and realizes informal Slack announcements won't work. They identify 12 key cross-functional connectors (department heads and team leads at integration points), secure CEO sponsorship first, build a standardized change playbook, and deliberately exclude the R&D team (who aren't affected) from the rollout scope—reducing the effective network to ~80 people and cutting the relationship count by over 95%.
